sections.title: Introduction: Data, Information and the IPO Cycle

blocks.text: A computer is an electronic machine that accepts raw facts, works on them according to a set of stored instructions, and gives back a result you can use. That three-part movement — take data in, process it, hand information out — is the single idea the whole of this chapter builds on, and it is why the machine is called a computer rather than a calculator or a filing cabinet.

Everything a computer does, from adding two numbers to streaming a film, reduces to that cycle. The chapters that follow will fill in each part: what the processing unit actually is, where the instructions live, how the results get to you.

blocks.caption: The input–process–output (IPO) cycle: every computer task follows it

blocks.text: Raw, unorganised facts and figures — marks in a register, temperatures logged by a sensor, the digits you type into a form. On its own, data carries no meaning.
Data that has been processed, organised and given context so that it is meaningful and useful — a class average, a weather forecast, a bank statement.

The distinction matters more than it sounds. A list of 400 numbers is data; the same list sorted, averaged and labelled "Class 11 Physics results" is information, and it is information you can act on. The computer's job is to make that transformation quickly and without error.
The IPO cycle in detail

items: Input — the input unit accepts data and instructions from the outside world and converts them into a form the machine can use. A keystroke becomes a binary code; a photograph becomes a grid of numbers.
Process — the central processing unit carries out arithmetic and logical operations on that data, following the instructions held in memory. This is where data becomes information.
Output — the output unit converts the results back into a form a human can read: text on a screen, a printed page, sound from a speaker.

blocks.text: Most textbooks add a fourth element, storage, because the instructions and the results have to live somewhere between the steps. That is why the fuller picture is sometimes drawn as input–process–output–storage, but the three-part version remains the useful way to think about what the machine is for.

Open a text editor and ask the class to name the input, process and output for typing a letter. Then ask what happens if the power fails before saving — that leads naturally into primary versus secondary memory later in the chapter.

sections.title: Definition, Characteristics and Application of Computer

blocks.text: A computer can be defined by what it does rather than what it looks like: it is a programmable electronic device that accepts input, stores and processes data according to a stored program, and produces output — all without human intervention once the program is running.
An electronic device that operates on data under the control of a stored program, performing the operations automatically at high speed and with accuracy.
Characteristics of a computer
Six characteristics separate a computer from other machines you use every day. They are worth memorising because exam questions ask for them directly, and each one explains a real design decision.

head: Characteristic
What it means
Why it matters in practice
rows: Operations are counted in millions or billions per second.
A payroll that takes a clerk a week is finished in seconds.
Results are exact, provided the input and the program are correct.
The machine does not make arithmetic slips — but it will faithfully repeat a bad instruction.
It works for hours without fatigue, boredom or loss of concentration.
Unlike a human, the ten-thousandth calculation is as careful as the first.
The same hardware performs entirely different tasks under different programs.
One laptop is a typewriter, a cinema, a calculator and a telephone.
Vast quantities of data can be held and recalled instantly.
The school's entire record system fits on a device in a pocket.
Once instructed, it runs the whole task without further human help.
A backup job can run at 2 a.m. with nobody present.

blocks.title: Garbage in, garbage out
blocks.text: Accuracy is conditional, not absolute. A computer will produce a wrong result just as confidently as a right one if it is given wrong data or a wrong program. The machine has no way to judge whether an instruction is sensible.
Applications of a computer
The chapter illustrates applications area by area. Learning two concrete uses per area is far more useful in an exam than learning a bare list of names.

blocks.caption: Computers in education: e-learning, research and record keeping
Computers in business: accounts, billing and stock control

items: Education — e-learning platforms, digital libraries, online examination, and school administration. Students can learn at their own pace and revisit material.
Business — accounting, invoicing, payroll, inventory and customer records. Spreadsheets make "what if" questions answerable in seconds.
Office — word processing, email, scheduling, and shared document work. The paperless office is still an ideal, but the paper-light office is normal.
Communication — email, voice and video calls, instant messaging and social media. Distance has stopped being a barrier to conversation.
Banking — ATM networks, online banking, electronic fund transfer, and fraud detection. Almost all money is now a number in a database.
Health and medicine — patient records, diagnostic imaging such as CT and MRI scans, monitoring equipment, and research.
Industry — automation, assembly-line robots, process control, and computer-aided design and manufacturing (CAD/CAM).
Military — simulation and training, logistics, navigation, and guidance systems.
Aviation — ticket reservation, air-traffic control, flight simulation, and the autopilot systems that fly the aircraft.
Robotics — machines that perform dangerous, repetitive or precise work, from welding car bodies to exploring other planets.
Graphics and design — illustration, animation, film effects, and desktop publishing.
Research — simulation, data analysis and modelling in every science, from weather forecasting to genetics.

blocks.caption: Computers in health: imaging, records and monitoring
Computers in industry: automation and process control
Computers in aviation: reservation, control and simulation

blocks.text: Ask each student to name one application they used before coming to class. Writing the answers on the board shows that "computer applications" is not a distant topic — it is the last hour of their own morning.

Computing did not begin with electronics. Every early device existed because someone needed to calculate faster or more reliably than they could by hand, and each one contributed an idea that survives in the machine on your desk.

head: Device
Who and when
The idea it contributed
rows: Position represents value — the first calculating aid, still used to teach place value.
Logarithmic scales turn multiplication into addition. Used by engineers until the 1970s.
A mechanical calculator using gears; could add and subtract directly.
Extended the gear machine to multiply and divide.
Wove patterns from punched cards — the first stored program was a set of holes in card.
The Analytical Engine had a mill (processor), a store (memory) and punched-card input — the architecture of a modern computer, designed a century before it could be built.
Processed the US census electrically; his company became IBM.
Stored-program concept: instructions and data share one memory. Almost every computer today is a von Neumann machine.
A large electromechanical computer using relays.

blocks.caption: The abacus — the earliest calculating aid
Blaise Pascal and his mechanical calculating machine
Charles Babbage with his Difference and Analytical Engine

blocks.title: Who was the first programmer?
blocks.text: Ada Lovelace wrote notes on the Analytical Engine in 1843, including a method for computing Bernoulli numbers — effectively the first published algorithm intended for a machine. That is why she is remembered as the first computer programmer.
Generations of computers
A generation marks a fundamental change in the underlying technology, not a modest improvement. Five are recognised, and each is defined by what the switching element is made of.

head: Generation
Period
Technology
Characteristics
Examples
rows: Enormous, consumed huge power, failed often, programmed in machine language.
Smaller, far more reliable, cooler; assembly language and early high-level languages such as FORTRAN and COBOL.
Many transistors on one chip; operating systems, multiprogramming, terminals.
A whole CPU on one chip; personal computers, GUIs, networks, the internet.
Intel 4004 onward, IBM PC, modern PCs
Parallel processing, natural language, machine learning, robotics.

blocks.caption: The switching technology that defines each generation

items: First generation used vacuum tubes — glass valves that glowed, ran hot and burned out regularly. A large machine might use tens of thousands of them and need constant maintenance.
Second generation replaced tubes with transistors: small, solid, cool and dependable. Size and power consumption fell by an order of magnitude.
Third generation put many transistors onto a single integrated circuit. This is when operating systems appeared, because the hardware finally became reliable enough to be worth sharing.
Fourth generation put the entire central processor onto one chip. That single step is why a computer fits in a pocket today.
Fifth generation is defined by what the machine can do rather than what it is made of — understanding language, learning from data, and reasoning.

blocks.caption: A schematic view of a fifth-generation system

blocks.text: Why is a Pentium a fourth-generation computer? Because its central processing unit is a microprocessor — a complete processor on a single chip. That is the defining technology of the fourth generation, regardless of the year it was sold.

Draw the generation table with the "technology" column blank and have students fill it in. The generation is defined by the switching element, and that single fact answers most exam questions on the topic.

sections.title: Measurement Unit of Processing Speed and Storage Unit

blocks.text: Two kinds of unit are easily confused and are frequently examined together: units of processing speed and units of storage. Speed is measured in events per second; storage is measured in bits and bytes.
Units of processing speed

head: Unit
Value
Meaning
rows: The base unit of clock frequency.
Thousands of millions of cycles per second — the everyday unit for a modern CPU clock.
A rough measure of how much work the processor completes.
Used for scientific work; supercomputers are rated in teraflops and petaflops.

blocks.text: The clock is a pulse that keeps every part of the processor in step. A 3 GHz clock ticks three thousand million times a second. A higher clock does not automatically mean a faster computer, because different processors do different amounts of work per tick — but within one family of processors it is a fair comparison.
Units of storage
A binary digit — a single 0 or 1. The smallest unit of data a computer can hold.
A group of eight bits. Enough to represent one character, which is why it became the standard unit.
Half a byte — four bits.
The number of bits a processor handles as a single unit — commonly 32 or 64 bits on modern machines.

blocks.title: Why 1,024 and not 1,000?
blocks.text: Computers count in binary, and 1,024 is 2¹⁰. Storage manufacturers often use the decimal values (1 KB = 1,000 bytes) instead, which is why a "500 GB" drive shows rather less than 500 GB when you connect it.
How many bits are in 2 KB? 2 KB = 2 × 1,024 bytes = 2,048 bytes, and each byte is 8 bits, so 2,048 × 8 = 16,384 bits.
Computers are classified by size, cost, speed and capacity. The boundaries have blurred — today's laptop outperforms yesterday's supercomputer — but the categories are still used and still examined.

head: Type
Scale
Typical use
Distinguishing feature
rows: Weather forecasting, nuclear simulation, cryptography, scientific research
Thousands of processors working in parallel; measures speed in FLOPS.
Banks, airlines, government — bulk transaction processing
Handles enormous input/output volume and many simultaneous users.
Supports many users at once; cheaper than a mainframe.
A single microprocessor; the personal computer.

blocks.caption: A supercomputer
A mainframe computer
A minicomputer

blocks.text: Classifying by working principle
A second scheme classifies computers by how they represent data, and it cross-cuts the size classification entirely.

items: Analog computer — works on continuously varying physical quantities such as voltage or temperature. It measures rather than counts. A speedometer and a mercury thermometer are analog devices.

Digital computer — works on discrete values, counting in binary 0 and 1. Every computer in ordinary use today is digital, because digital data can be copied and transmitted without any loss of accuracy.
Hybrid computer — combines both, converting analog signals from the physical world into digital form for processing. Used in hospitals for intensive-care monitoring and in industrial process control.

blocks.caption: Analog computer (left) and digital computer (right)
A hybrid computer — analog inputs converted for digital processing

blocks.text: Portable microcomputers
Within the microcomputer class, portability produced a family of names that exam questions like to distinguish.

head: Type
Description
rows: Designed to stay on a desk; mains powered, largest screen and keyboard.
A portable computer with a folding screen, keyboard and battery in one unit.
A flat touchscreen device with no physical keyboard.
Small enough to hold in one hand; largely superseded by smartphones.
A high-performance single-user machine for technical or scientific work — more powerful than a desktop PC.

blocks.text: Bring a phone, a tablet and a laptop to class if possible. Asking "which of these is a microcomputer?" (all of them) and "which is a workstation?" (none) fixes the vocabulary faster than a table does.
Using a portable computing device while connected to a network, so that the user can work from anywhere rather than at one fixed place.

Mobile computing is the combination of three things: portable hardware, wireless connectivity, and software designed for a small screen and an intermittent connection. Remove any one of them and you have a laptop, a network, or an app — but not mobile computing.
Features of mobile computing

items: Portability — the device travels with the user and works on battery power.
Connectivity — Wi-Fi, mobile data and Bluetooth keep the device on the network while it moves.
Location awareness — GPS and network positioning let applications respond to where the user is.
Always on — the device is carried switched on and reachable all day.
Touch and sensors — gesture input, camera, accelerometer and compass replace the mouse and keyboard.

blocks.text: Applications

items: Communication — voice and video calls, messaging and email from anywhere.
Mobile banking and payment — transferring money and paying by phone, which has transformed commerce in countries where banks are far away.
Navigation — turn-by-turn directions using live position and traffic data.
Health — fitness tracking, appointment reminders and remote consultation.
Education — learning material available to students who cannot reach a library.
Field work — surveys, deliveries and inspections recorded on the spot instead of on paper.

blocks.text: Advantages and limitations

head: Advantages
Limitations
rows: Work from anywhere, at any time
Small screens restrict what can be read and typed
Battery life limits how long the device stays useful
Wireless networks are not available everywhere and can be slow
Cheaper than a desktop for many tasks
Greater risk of loss, theft and interception of data
Less suited to long or heavy work such as programming or video editing

blocks.text: Compare a mobile payment with a bank visit. It makes the advantages concrete, and it leads directly into the cyber-security chapter, which is where the limitations get their answer.

sections.title: Concept of Computer Architecture and Organization

blocks.text: The design of a computer as the programmer sees it: the instruction set, the data formats, the addressing modes and the registers.
How the architecture is actually built in hardware: the physical units, the connections between them, and the control signals that drive them.

The distinction is between "what the machine appears to do" and "how it is made to do it". Two processors can share an architecture — the same instructions, the same registers — while being organised completely differently inside. Architecture is a contract with the programmer; organization is an engineering choice.

Almost every computer in use follows the von Neumann architecture, named after John von Neumann's 1945 report. Its central idea is the stored program: instructions are held in memory in exactly the same way as data, so a program is itself data that can be read, written and modified. Before this, programming a machine meant rewiring it.

blocks.caption: The elements of a computer system and its logical structure

blocks.text: The five functional units

items: Input unit — accepts data and instructions and converts them to machine-readable form.
Memory / storage unit — holds both the instructions and the data, and the results until they are needed.
Arithmetic and logic unit (ALU) — performs the arithmetic and the comparisons.
Control unit — reads instructions from memory, interprets them and directs the other units to carry them out.
Output unit — converts results back into a form a human can use.

blocks.caption: Block diagram of the major components of a computer system

blocks.text: The control unit and the ALU together form the central processing unit. The CPU is the part that people mean when they say "the computer" — but it can do nothing without memory to hold its instructions and without input and output to connect it to the world.
Trace one instruction through the diagram: fetch from memory, decode in the control unit, execute in the ALU, store the result. Students who can narrate that cycle have understood the architecture.
A computer system is not only the box. It is the hardware, the software, the data and the people who use it, and a problem with any one of them makes the whole system fail.

head: Component
What it is
Examples
rows: The physical, touchable parts of the system.
The programs and instructions that tell the hardware what to do.
The raw material the software works on.
A class register, a photograph, a spreadsheet
The agreed rules for using the system.

blocks.text: Software that is permanently stored in read-only memory — for example the BIOS or UEFI that starts a PC before the operating system loads. It is called firmware because it sits between hardware and software.

The three words hardware, software and firmware are asked about together, and the difference is simply permanence. Hardware you can drop on your foot. Software you can change or delete. Firmware is software that has been fixed into a chip so that it survives the power being switched off.
The CPU and its parts

items: Control unit — fetches instructions, decodes them and issues control signals. It does not process data itself; it directs everyone else.
ALU — carries out arithmetic (add, subtract, multiply, divide) and logical operations (compare, AND, OR, NOT).
Registers — a handful of very fast storage locations inside the CPU that hold the instruction being worked on and the data it needs.

blocks.title: Cache
blocks.text: Registers are the fastest storage in a computer and also the smallest. Main memory is larger and slower; disk is larger still and slower again. Cache memory exists to bridge that gap — see the memory section below.
A complete central processing unit fabricated on a single integrated-circuit chip. It contains the control unit, the ALU and registers.
Putting the whole processor on one chip is the single development that made personal computing possible. Everything else in the fourth generation follows from it.
Characteristics of a microprocessor

head: Term
Meaning
Why it matters
rows: The rate of the clock pulse that synchronises operations, in MHz or GHz.
Sets how fast instructions are stepped through. Compare only within one processor family.
The number of bits the processor handles at once — 8, 16, 32, 64.
A wider word moves and processes more data per operation.
How many bits travel along the data bus at once.
Affects how quickly data moves between the CPU and memory.
The complete set of operations the processor understands.
Defines what software can ask the machine to do.
Independent processing units on one chip.
More cores allow genuinely simultaneous work.

items: Clock speed is measured in hertz. A 3.2 GHz processor steps 3.2 thousand million times a second.
Word length determines the largest number the processor can handle in one operation. Moving from 32-bit to 64-bit is what allowed computers to use more than 4 GB of memory directly.
Cores let a processor do several things at once rather than rapidly switching between them.

blocks.text: Well-known microprocessor families include the Intel x86 series (8086, 80286, 80386, 80486, Pentium, Core i3/i5/i7/i9), the AMD Ryzen and Athlon ranges, the ARM processors that power almost every phone and tablet, and the Apple Silicon chips in recent Macs.
A set of parallel wires that carries signals between the parts of a computer. Three buses do three different jobs.

head: Bus
Carries
Direction
Effect of width
rows: More lines means more bits moved per transfer
The address of the memory location or device
Determines how much memory can be addressed
Timing and control signals — read, write, interrupt, clock

blocks.caption: Bus architecture: data, address and control buses linking the units

blocks.text: An analogy helps. The address bus is the street name on an envelope, the data bus is the letter inside it, and the control bus is the postal service that decides when to deliver and collect. Without the address bus the data has nowhere to go; without the control bus nothing knows when to move.

blocks.title: Address bus and memory size
blocks.text: With n address lines, the processor can address 2ⁿ distinct locations. A 32-bit address bus addresses 2³² locations — about 4 GB. That limit is exactly why 64-bit processors became necessary.
The part of a computer that holds instructions and data so that the processor can reach them.
Memory is arranged as a hierarchy: the faster it is, the smaller and more expensive it is. The whole art of memory design is putting the right data in the right level of that hierarchy.

blocks.caption: The memory hierarchy — fastest and smallest at the top

blocks.text: Primary memory
Read/write memory that holds the programs and data currently in use. It is volatile — everything in it is lost when the power goes off.
Memory whose contents are fixed during manufacture. It is non-volatile, so it survives switching off, and it holds the startup instructions the machine needs before anything else is available.

items: SRAM (static RAM) holds its contents as long as power is supplied, with no need to refresh. It is fast and expensive, and is used for cache.
DRAM (dynamic RAM) stores each bit as charge in a capacitor that leaks away, so it must be refreshed thousands of times a second. It is slower and much cheaper, and is used for main memory.

blocks.caption: RAM — read/write primary memory
ROM — non-volatile memory holding startup instructions

blocks.text: Types of ROM

head: Type
Full form
How it is programmed
rows: Written once by the user, then fixed.
Erased by ultraviolet light, then reprogrammed.
Erased and rewritten electrically, byte by byte — the basis of flash memory.

blocks.text: Whether memory loses its contents when power is removed. RAM is volatile; ROM, flash and disks are not.
Cache memory
A small, very fast memory between the processor and main memory that holds copies of the data and instructions used most recently.

Cache works because programs do not access memory at random — they repeatedly use the same small set of instructions and data. Keeping a copy of that working set next to the processor removes most of the waiting. A cache hit is served at processor speed; a miss has to go to main memory.

blocks.caption: Relationship between cache, primary memory and secondary memory

blocks.text: Why is cache useful? The processor is far faster than main memory, so without cache it would spend most of its time idle, waiting. Cache supplies the data it is most likely to ask for next, so the processor keeps working instead of stalling.
Flash memory

Flash is a form of EEPROM: non-volatile, electrically erasable and rewritten in blocks rather than byte by byte. It is what makes pen drives, memory cards and solid-state drives possible — storage with no moving parts.

blocks.caption: Flash memory — non-volatile, no moving parts

blocks.text: Non-volatile storage outside the main memory, used to hold programs and data permanently. It is slower than primary memory but vastly larger and far cheaper per byte.
Primary memory alone cannot work: it forgets everything the moment the machine is switched off, and it is too expensive to hold everything you own. Secondary storage is the permanent record.
Magnetic storage
A disk coated with a material that can be magnetised in tiny regions; each region stores a bit. Reading and writing is done by a head that moves over the spinning surface.

blocks.caption: Inside a hard disk: platters, spindle and read/write head

items: Hard disk drive (HDD) — a stack of rigid platters spinning at thousands of revolutions per minute, with a head flying just above the surface. Large and cheap per gigabyte, but mechanical and therefore comparatively slow and shock-sensitive.
Floppy disk — a flexible plastic disk in a protective sleeve, once the standard way to carry files. Obsolete: it held 1.44 MB, less than a single photograph today.
Magnetic tape — a long ribbon of coated plastic, read sequentially. Far too slow for everyday work, but still used for archival backup because it is cheap and lasts for decades.

blocks.caption: Magnetic tape — sequential access, used for archival backup

blocks.text: Solid-state and removable storage

head: Medium
How it works
Typical use today
rows: The main drive in most modern computers
Flash memory in a small portable case
Distribution of software and film; largely superseded
Obsolete — the name survives as a generic term

blocks.caption: A pen drive — flash memory in a portable case

blocks.text: Access methods
Data can only be reached by passing through everything before it, as on a tape. Reaching the last item means reading the whole length.
Any item can be reached directly and in roughly the same time, as on a disk or in RAM.
This is the crucial difference between tape and disk, and it is why tape is fine for backups that are read rarely and in full, but useless for running a program.

blocks.title: Why is a CD-ROM more reliable than a floppy?
blocks.text: A floppy is magnetic and its surface is exposed to dust, fingerprints and magnetic fields; it also fails if the drive mechanism is dirty. A CD-ROM is read by a laser that never touches the surface, and the data sits under a layer of plastic — so everyday handling does not damage it.
Any hardware that converts data from the outside world into a form the computer can process.
The chapter lists the devices below. For each one, know what it is for and one situation where it is the right choice — that is what exam questions actually test.

head: Device
Purpose
Used for
rows: An upside-down mouse: the ball is moved by hand
Finger movement on a flat surface moves the pointer
A lever that reports direction and tilt
Detects where the finger touches the display
A photosensitive pen that detects position on a CRT screen
Drawing directly on screen; now largely historical
A flat surface with a stylus that reports position and pressure
Converts a paper image into a digital image
Converts sound into an electrical signal
Reads the pattern of bars into a number
Optical Mark Recognition — detects pencil marks in fixed positions
Optical Character Recognition — converts an image of text into editable text
Magnetic Ink Character Recognition — reads characters printed in magnetic ink
Reads the chip embedded in a card
Identity cards, bank cards, SIM cards

blocks.caption: The keyboard — the standard text input device
The mouse — pointing device for graphical interfaces
A scanner converts a paper image into a digital image

blocks.title: OMR, OCR, MICR — how to keep them straight
blocks.text: All three read marks optically, but: OMR detects whether a box is filled in (a mark sheet); OCR recognises the shapes of letters and turns them into text; MICR reads magnetic ink, so it works reliably even if the cheque is stamped or dirty. Banks use MICR precisely because it is tamper-resistant.
If an OMR sheet is available, bring one. Students who have filled in an answer sheet understand OMR immediately, and the limitation — only marks in fixed positions can be read — becomes obvious.
Any hardware that converts processed results from machine form into a form a person can use.
Output displayed on a screen. It is immediate and editable, but temporary — it disappears when the machine is switched off.
Output printed on paper. It is permanent, portable and readable without a machine, but slow to produce and it consumes paper.
Monitors
A monitor is the standard soft-copy output device. The two technologies that exam questions compare are CRT and LCD.

head: Feature
CRT
LCD
rows: An electron beam scans a phosphor-coated glass tube
Liquid crystals control light passing through, with a backlight
Good; can look washed out at an angle

blocks.caption: A CRT monitor and its internal anatomy
An LCD monitor

blocks.text: Other display types worth knowing: LED monitors are LCD panels with light-emitting-diode backlighting — brighter and thinner, with better contrast; a plasma display uses small cells of ionised gas; a monochrome monitor shows a single colour, and a grayscale monitor shows shades of grey.
Printers
An output device that produces a hard copy of text and graphics on paper.
The first division is between impact and non-impact printers, and that division explains almost every other difference.

head: Feature
Impact printer
Non-impact printer
rows: Strikes an inked ribbon against the paper
No contact — ink is sprayed, fused or deposited
Dot matrix, daisy wheel, chain, drum

blocks.caption: A dot matrix printer — impact printing, character built from pins
An inkjet printer — non-impact, sprays droplets of ink
A laser printer — non-impact, toner fused by heat

items: Dot matrix builds each character from a grid of tiny pins striking a ribbon. It is slow and noisy, but it can print through carbon paper — which is why it survives in places that need multi-part forms.
Daisy wheel has the characters moulded on petals of a wheel; it strikes the right petal against the ribbon. Print quality is like a typewriter, but no graphics are possible.
Inkjet sprays microscopic droplets of ink onto the paper. Quiet, cheap to buy, excellent for photographs — but ink is expensive and the head can dry out.
Laser works like a photocopier: a laser draws the image as static charge on a drum, the drum picks up toner, and heat fuses the toner to the paper. Fast, sharp and quiet; the standard office printer.

blocks.text: Which printer uses a light beam and electrically sensitive black powder? The laser printer. The light beam is the laser, and the powder is the toner — a fine plastic powder that is attracted to the charged image and then fused by heat.
Other output devices

items: Speaker — converts digital audio into sound. Essential for multimedia, but of no use in a quiet library.
Plotter — draws with pens on large sheets. It is the right tool for maps, architectural plans and engineering drawings, where a printer cannot produce the size or the line quality.
Projector — throws the screen image onto a wall, for teaching and presentations.

blocks.caption: A plotter — for large, high-quality graphics and drawings

blocks.text: A socket on the outside of the system unit used to connect a peripheral device, transfer data, and — for low-power devices — supply electricity.
A port is the meeting point between the computer and the outside world. Choosing the wrong one means the device simply will not work, so the names and shapes matter.

head: Port
Data transfer
Typical use
Notes
rows: Simple and reliable over a long cable, but slow
Eight bits at a time, side by side
Faster than serial over a short distance; limited cable length
Nearly everything: keyboard, mouse, printer, storage, phone
Plug and play, hot-swappable, and supplies power
Fast and isochronous; largely replaced by USB 3 and Thunderbolt
Can chain several devices; largely superseded
Carries picture and sound on one cable
Requires the devices to see each other

blocks.caption: A serial port — one bit at a time
A parallel port — eight bits side by side
USB — the universal connection for modern peripherals
HDMI carries digital audio and video on one cable

blocks.text: Expansion slots
A socket on the motherboard that accepts an additional circuit board, adding capability the machine did not have when it was built.

Common examples are PCI for general expansion, PCI Express for modern graphics and high-speed cards, AGP for older graphics cards, and ISA on very old machines. A sound card, a network card or a dedicated graphics card is installed this way.

blocks.caption: PCI expansion slots on a motherboard
An expansion slot accepting an additional circuit board

blocks.text: Serial or parallel? Serial sends one bit at a time down one wire — slower in principle, but it works reliably over long distances and wiring is cheap. Parallel sends eight bits at once down eight wires — faster over a short cable, but the signals interfere with each other over distance, so cables must stay short. That is why modern high-speed connections such as USB and SATA are serial: at high speed, parallel wiring becomes the limiting factor.
Pass a USB cable and an HDMI cable round the class. Recognising the connectors by sight, and knowing what each carries, is more useful than memorising the pin counts.
