short.q: Why the computer is known as versatile and diligent device? Explain.
short.a:
Versatile because the same hardware performs completely different tasks under different programs — one machine is a typewriter, a cinema, a calculator and a telephone. Nothing about the hardware changes between those uses; only the instructions it is given.

Diligent because it does not tire, get bored or lose concentration. The ten-thousandth calculation is performed with the same care as the first, which is why computers are given repetitive work that people do badly.

short.q: What are the application areas of the computer? Explain in brief.
short.a: Education — e-learning, digital libraries, online examination. Business — accounts, payroll, inventory. Office — word processing, email, scheduling. Communication — email, video calls, social media. Banking — ATMs, online banking, fraud detection. Health — records, CT and MRI imaging. Industry — automation, robots, CAD/CAM. Military — simulation, logistics, guidance. Aviation — reservation, air-traffic control, autopilot. Also robotics, graphics and design, and scientific research.

short.q: Why is Charles Babbage known as ‘Father of the Computer’?
short.a:
Babbage designed the Analytical Engine in 1837, a machine with a mill (the processor), a store (the memory), and punched-card input and output — that is, the architecture of a modern computer, conceived a century before the electronics existed to build it.

He is called the father of the computer because he established the idea: a general-purpose machine controlled by a stored program rather than a device built to do one calculation.

short.q: Describe at least five ways in which information technology can help students studying subjects other than computing.
short.a:
1. Reference material — encyclopedias, journals and primary sources far beyond what a school library holds.

2. Simulation — a chemistry student can run a reaction that would be dangerous or slow in a school laboratory.

3. Visualisation — three-dimensional models in biology, geometry and astronomy that cannot be drawn on a board.

4. Data analysis — a geography or economics student can work with real datasets and see the pattern in a chart.

5. Language learning — pronunciation, listening practice and conversation with material that native speakers produced.

6. Collaboration — shared documents let a group write one piece of work together.

short.q: Why is John Von Neumann a remarkable name in the history of the computer?
short.a:
Because of the stored-program concept described in his 1945 report on the EDVAC. Before it, programming a machine meant rewiring it. von Neumann's idea was that instructions should be held in memory in exactly the same way as data, so a program becomes data that the machine can read and modify.

Almost every computer built since is a von Neumann machine, and the bottleneck created by sharing one memory between instructions and data is still called the von Neumann bottleneck.

short.q: Write brief note on the achievement of the following computer scientists: a. Howard Aiken b. Herman Hollerith c. Lady Ada
short.a:
Howard Aiken — built the Mark-I in 1944, a large electromechanical computer using relays.

Herman Hollerith — developed the punched-card tabulating machine that processed the 1890 US census in a fraction of the time a manual count would have taken. His company later became IBM.

Lady Ada Lovelace — wrote notes on Babbage's Analytical Engine in 1843, including a method for computing Bernoulli numbers. It is effectively the first published algorithm intended for a machine, which is why she is remembered as the first computer programmer.

short.q: Explain the evolution of the computer describing the technologies used in different generations.
short.a:
Computing developed from manual aids to electronic machines, each stage contributing an idea that survives: the abacus (position represents value), the slide rule (logarithms turn multiplication into addition), Pascal's gear-driven calculator, Leibniz's Stepped Reckoner, Jacquard's punched-card loom, Babbage's Analytical Engine, Hollerith's tabulating machine, and finally the EDVAC with von Neumann's stored-program concept.

The five generations are then defined by their switching technology: vacuum tubes, transistors, integrated circuits, microprocessors, and artificial intelligence.

short.q: What do you mean by generation of computers? Explain the characteristics of third generation of computers.
short.a:
A generation is a stage of development marked by a fundamental change in the underlying technology, specifically in the component used for switching.

The third generation (1964–1971) used integrated circuits — many transistors on one chip. Characteristics: much smaller and cheaper than transistor machines; far more reliable, which for the first time made it sensible to share the machine, so operating systems, multiprogramming and terminals appeared; users worked through keyboards and monitors rather than punched cards. The IBM System/360 is the representative machine.

short.q: Compare and contrast between first and second generations of computers.
short.a:
First generation (1940–1956) used vacuum tubes: enormous, consuming huge power, failing frequently, programmed in machine language. Examples: ENIAC, EDVAC, UNIVAC-I.

Second generation (1956–1963) used transistors: small, solid, cool and dependable. Size and power consumption fell by an order of magnitude, reliability improved enormously, and assembly language and early high-level languages such as FORTRAN and COBOL appeared. Examples: IBM 1401, IBM 7090.

short.q: Differentiate between second and third generation of computers.
short.a:
Second generation used transistors — discrete components, one per package. Machines were smaller and far more reliable than tube machines, and used assembly language and early high-level languages.

Third generation used integrated circuits — many transistors fabricated on one chip. This brought another large fall in size and cost, and crucially the hardware became reliable enough to be worth sharing, so operating systems and multiprogramming appeared.

short.q: Describe the major characteristics of fourth generation computers.
short.a:
The fourth generation (1971–present) is defined by the microprocessor — a complete CPU on a single chip.

Characteristics: very small size and low cost, which produced the personal computer; graphical user interfaces, so no programming knowledge is needed to operate one; networking, which gave us the internet; very large memory and storage; and high reliability. Examples: the Intel 4004 onward, the IBM PC, and every modern computer.

short.q: Explain the technologies used in different generations of computers.
short.a: First: vacuum tubes — glass valves that glowed, ran hot and burned out often. Second: transistors — small, solid, cool, dependable. Third: integrated circuits — many transistors on one chip. Fourth: microprocessors — a whole CPU on one chip. Fifth: artificial intelligence — defined by capability rather than by component, using parallel processing and machine learning.

short.q: Compare the distinctions between third and fourth generations of computers.
short.a:
Third generation used integrated circuits: many transistors on one chip, but the processor was still built from several chips. Operating systems and multiprogramming appeared; machines were shared and expensive.

Fourth generation put the entire processor on one chip. That step is what made the personal computer possible — a computer became something an individual could own rather than an organisation had to share.

short.q: Pentium I computers are fourth generation computers. Why?
short.a: Because the Pentium's central processing unit is a microprocessor — a complete processor on a single chip. That is the defining technology of the fourth generation, and it applies regardless of when the machine was sold.

short.q: What are the advantages of transistors over vacuum tubes?
short.a: Transistors are far smaller, need much less power, run cool rather than glowing, are far more reliable with no filament to burn out, have a much longer life, are cheaper to produce in quantity, and switch much faster.

short.q: Write short notes on: a. Charles Babbage b. AI c. EDVAC d. Abacus e. Evolution of the computer
short.a:
Charles Babbage — designed the Difference Engine and, in 1837, the Analytical Engine with a mill, a store and punched-card input: the architecture of a modern computer.

AI (Artificial Intelligence) — the field concerned with making machines perform tasks that need human-like intelligence: understanding language, learning from data, reasoning. It defines the fifth generation.

EDVAC — Electronic Discrete Variable Automatic Computer; the machine described in von Neumann's 1945 report and the first designed around the stored-program concept.

Abacus — the earliest calculating aid, using beads on rods where position represents value.

Evolution of the computer — from the abacus through mechanical calculators, punched-card machines and Babbage's designs to the electronic stored-program machines of today, with each generation marked by a change in switching technology.

short.q: Compare and contrast Analogue and Digital computers with appropriate examples.
short.a:
An analog computer works on continuously varying physical quantities such as voltage or temperature; it measures. Examples: a speedometer, a mercury thermometer, an old slide rule.

A digital computer works on discrete values, counting in binary 0 and 1; it counts. Every computer in ordinary use is digital.

The decisive difference is accuracy: a digital value can be copied and transmitted any number of times without any loss, whereas an analog value picks up a little noise every time it is copied. That is why audio, video and telephony all went digital.

short.q: Briefly define the hybrid computer with its application areas.
short.a:
A hybrid computer combines analog and digital processing: it takes analog signals from the physical world, converts them to digital form for processing, and often converts the result back.

Applications: hospital intensive care, where it monitors a patient's analog vital signs and alarms digitally; industrial process control, where it reads sensors and adjusts machinery; and scientific instruments that digitise measurements.

short.q: What are super computers? Explain their applications in real life situation.
short.a:
A supercomputer is the fastest and most powerful class of computer, built by running thousands of processors in parallel and rated in FLOPS (floating-point operations per second).

Applications: weather forecasting and climate modelling; nuclear and scientific simulation; drug discovery and molecular modelling; cryptanalysis; oil and gas exploration; and modelling airflow over aircraft and vehicles.

short.q: Why is a supercomputer not easily available like other computers?
short.a: Because of cost — millions of dollars to buy, and comparable amounts to run. Because of infrastructure: the power supply and the cooling needed are those of a small factory, not an office. Because of specialist operation: they need teams of engineers to keep them running. And because there is little demand — the work that justifies one exists only in national laboratories, large research universities and a few industries.

short.q: Describe the major features of the super computer.
short.a: Extremely high processing speed measured in teraflops or petaflops; massive parallelism, with thousands of processors working together; very large, very fast memory; high-speed interconnects between the processors; sophisticated cooling; and enormous cost and power consumption. They are built for throughput on large numerical problems rather than for responsiveness to one user.

short.q: Which of the following printers uses light beam and electrostatically sensitive black powder?
short.a: The laser printer. The light beam is the laser, and the powder is the toner — a fine plastic powder that is attracted to the electrostatically charged image on the drum and then fused to the paper by heat.

short.q: Impact printers . . . .
short.a: Impact printers strike a ribbon against the paper to produce character images. That is why they are noisy, slower than non-impact printers, and lower in quality — but also why they can print through carbon paper to make multi-part forms, which no non-impact printer can do.

short.q: Describe the Mainframe computer in detail.
short.a:
A mainframe is a large, powerful computer designed to handle enormous volumes of input and output for many simultaneous users. Where a supercomputer is built for raw calculation, a mainframe is built for transaction throughput and reliability.

Features: it supports hundreds or thousands of concurrent users; it has extensive redundancy, so a component can fail without the system stopping; it can run for years without interruption; and it handles very large databases with strong security.

Uses: banks processing transactions, airlines running reservation systems, government departments holding citizen records, and large-scale payroll.

short.q: What are the advantages and limitations of mainframes over the minicomputer?
short.a:
Advantages. Far greater processing power and memory; much higher input/output capacity, so it handles far more transactions; supports many more simultaneous users; more reliable, with redundancy built in; and stronger security and auditing.

Limitations. Far more expensive to buy and to run; needs specialist staff to operate; needs a controlled environment with dedicated power and cooling; takes up a great deal of space; and is uneconomic below a certain scale of work.

short.q: Differentiate between Mini and Mainframe computer.
short.a:
A minicomputer is mid-range: it serves a department or controls a process, supports tens of users, and is modest in cost and size.

A mainframe is the largest class used for bulk transaction work: it supports hundreds or thousands of users, has very high input/output capacity, extensive redundancy and strong security, and costs very much more.

short.q: What is mobile computing? Explain.
short.a:
Mobile computing is using a portable computing device while connected to a network, so that work is not tied to one fixed place.

It depends on three things together: portable hardware, wireless connectivity, and software designed for a small screen and an intermittent connection. Remove any one and you have a laptop, a network, or an app — but not mobile computing.

short.q: List out the major features of mobile computing.
short.a: Portability — the device travels with the user on battery power. Connectivity — Wi-Fi, mobile data and Bluetooth keep it on the network while it moves. Location awareness — GPS and network positioning. Always on — carried switched on and reachable all day. Touch and sensors — gesture input, camera, accelerometer and compass replace the mouse and keyboard.

short.q: Explain the advantages of mobile computing.
short.a: Work happens from anywhere at any time; communication is immediate; location-aware services become possible; it removes paperwork and delay, since data is recorded on the spot; and for many tasks it is cheaper than providing a desktop for everyone.

short.q: Explain the importance of mobile computing.
short.a: It has extended computing to people and places that desktops never reached. Mobile banking brings financial services to areas with no branch. Field workers — surveyors, health workers, delivery drivers — record data where it happens instead of transcribing it later. Students reach material without a library. In countries where fixed infrastructure is thin, the mobile phone is the first computer most people own, so mobile computing is not a convenience but the main route to digital services.

short.q: Write short notes on: a. Microcomputer b. Super Computer c. Analog computer d. IBM PC and IBM Compatibles e. Digital Computers f. Workstation g. Mobile computing
short.a:
Microcomputer — a computer built around a single microprocessor; the personal computer.

Supercomputer — the fastest class, using massive parallelism for scientific work; measured in FLOPS.

Analog computer — works on continuously varying physical quantities; it measures rather than counts.

IBM PC and IBM Compatibles — the IBM PC of 1981 set the standard for the personal computer, and "compatibles" were other manufacturers' machines built to the same open specification, which is why the PC architecture became universal.

Digital computer — works on discrete binary values; the ordinary modern computer.

Workstation — a high-performance single-user machine for technical or scientific work, more powerful than a desktop PC.

Mobile computing — using a portable device while connected to a network, so work is not tied to one place.

short.q: Distinguish among the terms, ‘hardware’, ‘software’ and ‘firmware’.
short.a:
Hardware is the physical equipment — you can drop it on your foot: keyboard, processor, disk.

Software is the programs and instructions that tell the hardware what to do. It has no physical form of its own, and you can change or delete it.

Firmware is software permanently fixed into a chip so that it survives switching off — the startup code of a PC, for example. It sits between the two: it is software, but it cannot be changed by ordinary means.

short.q: Explain the functions of the CPU.
short.a:
The CPU fetches each instruction from memory, decodes it to work out what is being asked, executes it — performing arithmetic or comparisons in the ALU, or moving data — and stores the result. It then moves to the next instruction.

Beyond that cycle it coordinates the other units through control signals, responds to interrupts from devices, and keeps everything in step with the clock.

short.q: Explain the work done by control unit and the ALU of the computer.
short.a:
The control unit directs: it fetches instructions, decodes them, and issues the control signals that make the other units act. It processes no data itself — it is the director, not the worker.

The ALU (Arithmetic and Logic Unit) does the work: arithmetic — addition, subtraction, multiplication, division — and logical operations such as comparisons, AND, OR and NOT. Its results are held in the accumulator.

short.q: What is memory? Differentiate between primary and secondary memory.
short.a:
Memory is the part of a computer that holds instructions and data so that the processor can reach them.

Primary memory (RAM, ROM, cache) is fast, directly accessible to the processor, smaller, more expensive per byte, and — in RAM's case — volatile.

Secondary memory (disks, SSDs, optical media) is non-volatile, much larger, far cheaper per byte, and much slower; it is not accessed directly by the processor but via input/output channels.

short.q: What is the importance of primary and secondary memory in a computer system?
short.a:
Primary memory is what makes execution possible at all: the processor can only work on data that is in it, and its speed sets how fast programs run.

Secondary memory is what makes the work permanent: it retains programs and data when the power is off, and it holds far more than primary memory could afford to.

A computer needs both — one without primary memory cannot run anything, and one without secondary memory forgets everything when switched off.

short.q: What is memory? Explain main memory and secondary memory.
short.a:
Memory holds the instructions and data a computer is working with.

Main (primary) memory is the working store the processor addresses directly: RAM for the running programs and their data, and ROM holding the fixed startup instructions. It is fast and volatile.

Secondary memory is long-term storage — hard disks, solid-state drives, optical discs and pen drives. It is non-volatile, far larger and cheaper per byte, but much slower.

short.q: What do you mean by ‘Volatility’? Explain RAM and ROM with the concept and term.
short.a:
Volatility is whether memory loses its contents when the power is removed.

RAM (Random Access Memory) is volatile — read/write, holding the programs and data currently in use, and losing everything when the machine is switched off. It comes in static form (SRAM, used for cache) and dynamic form (DRAM, used for main memory).

ROM (Read-Only Memory) is non-volatile — written during manufacture and not changed afterwards, so it survives switching off and holds the startup instructions the machine needs before anything else is available. Variants include PROM, EPROM and EEPROM.

short.q: Differentiate between RAM and ROM.
short.a:
RAM is read/write and volatile; it holds the running programs and their data, and the user changes its contents constantly.

ROM is read-only and non-volatile; it holds fixed startup instructions, and its contents are not changed in normal use.

RAM is larger and is where the work happens; ROM is smaller and is how the machine knows how to begin.

short.q: Differentiate between Static RAM and Dynamic RAM. Write full form of PROM, EPROM and EEPROM.
short.a:
SRAM (static RAM) holds its contents as long as power is supplied, with no refreshing needed. It is fast and expensive, and is used for cache.

DRAM (dynamic RAM) stores each bit as charge in a capacitor that leaks away, so it must be refreshed thousands of times a second. It is slower and much cheaper, and is used for main memory.

PROM — Programmable Read-Only Memory. EPROM — Erasable Programmable Read-Only Memory (erased with ultraviolet light). EEPROM — Electrically Erasable Programmable Read-Only Memory (erased and rewritten electrically; the basis of flash memory).

short.q: What do you understand by storage media? Why is CD-ROM more reliable than the floppy disk?
short.a:
Storage media are the physical materials on which data is recorded: magnetic disks and tapes, optical discs, and flash memory.

A CD-ROM is more reliable than a floppy because it is read by a laser that never touches the surface, and the data sits under a layer of plastic protected from dust, fingerprints and magnetic fields. A floppy is magnetic, its surface is exposed, and it is read by a head that can be dirty or misaligned. Handle both roughly and the floppy fails; the disc usually survives.

short.q: What is a cache memory? Why is it useful in computer system?
short.a:
Cache is a small, very fast memory between the processor and main memory, holding copies of the instructions and data used most recently.

It is useful because the processor is far faster than main memory, and without cache it would spend most of its time idle, waiting. It works because programs do not access memory at random — they repeatedly use the same small working set, so keeping that set next to the processor removes most of the waiting.

short.q: What do you mean by data sequencing? Differentiate between random access and sequential access.
short.a:
Sequential access means data can only be reached by passing through everything before it, as on magnetic tape — reaching the last item means reading the whole length.

Random (direct) access means any item can be reached directly, in roughly the same time as any other, as on a disk or in RAM.

This is why tape is fine for backups read rarely and in full, but useless for running a program, which jumps about constantly.

short.q: Explain briefly the functions of input unit and control unit of a computer.
short.a:
The input unit accepts data and instructions from the outside world and converts them into a form the machine can use — a keystroke becomes a binary code, a photograph becomes a grid of numbers. It also passes the data to memory when the processor is ready for it.

The control unit fetches each instruction from memory, decodes it, and issues the control signals that direct the other units. It manages the fetch–decode–execute cycle and keeps the whole system in step.

short.q: What is the role of input and output devices in a computer system? Name some of the input and output devices used with computers and explain two of them.
short.a:
Their role is to connect the computer to the world: input devices convert what a person supplies into machine-readable form, and output devices convert results back into a form a person can use. Without them a computer cannot be told anything or report anything.

Input: keyboard, mouse, scanner, microphone, digital camera, joystick, touch screen, OMR, OCR, MICR, bar-code reader.

Output: monitor, printer, speaker, projector, plotter.

The keyboard is the standard text input device: each key closes a circuit, and the keyboard's own controller converts that into a binary code the computer receives.

The monitor is the standard soft-copy output device. An LCD panel controls light passing through liquid crystals, so a signal can switch each tiny region between dark and transparent, building the picture.

short.q: Write short notes on touch pads and light pens.
short.a:
Touch pad — a flat, pressure- or capacitance-sensitive surface, built into laptops, that converts finger movement into pointer movement. It replaces the mouse where there is no desk.

Light pen — a photosensitive pen that detects the position on a screen by sensing the light emitted as the electron beam passes. It let a user draw directly on a CRT. It worked only with CRT technology and is now largely historical, its role taken by touch screens and graphics tablets.

short.q: What is the printer? Differentiate between softcopy and hardcopy output.
short.a:
A printer is an output device that produces a permanent copy of text and graphics on paper.

Soft copy is output shown on a screen: immediate, editable and searchable, but temporary — it disappears when the machine is switched off unless saved.

Hard copy is output on paper: permanent, portable, readable without a machine, and accepted as a record — but slow to produce and it consumes paper.

short.q: Differentiate between Impact printer and Non-impact printer.
short.a:
An impact printer forms characters by striking an inked ribbon against the paper: noisy, slow, lower quality, but able to print through carbon paper for multi-part forms. Examples: dot matrix, daisy wheel.

A non-impact printer puts the image on paper without contact — by spraying ink, fusing toner or heating paper: quiet, fast and high quality, but unable to make carbon copies. Examples: inkjet, laser, thermal.

short.q: What is an output? Distinguish between CRT monitor and LCD monitor.
short.a:
Output is the processed result that a computer produces and presents in a form a person can use.

A CRT fires an electron beam at a phosphor-coated tube. It gives excellent colour and viewing angle, but it is deep, heavy, power-hungry and can flicker.

An LCD controls light passing through liquid crystals with a backlight. It is thin, light and low-power, with no flicker — though contrast can fall off when viewed at an angle.

short.q: What is a BUS in computer architecture?
short.a:
A bus is a set of parallel wires that carries signals between the parts of a computer. Three buses do three different jobs: the data bus carries the actual value, the address bus carries where it is to go, and the control bus carries the timing signals that say when.

An analogy: the address bus is the street name on an envelope, the data bus is the letter inside, and the control bus is the postal service that decides when to deliver.

short.q: Describe the differences between serial and parallel interfaces.
short.a:
Serial sends one bit at a time down one wire. It is slower in principle, but the wiring is cheap and simple and it works reliably over long distances — which is why high-speed modern connections such as USB and SATA are serial.

Parallel sends several bits at once down several wires — eight at a time on a classic parallel port. It is faster over a short cable, but at high speed the signals interfere with one another (crosstalk) and must stay in step, so cables have to be short. That limitation is why parallel gave way to serial.

short.q: What do you mean by microprocessor? Write the name of some popular microprocessors.
short.a:
A microprocessor is a complete central processing unit fabricated on a single integrated-circuit chip, containing the control unit, the ALU and registers. Putting the whole processor on one chip is the development that made personal computing possible.

Examples: the Intel x86 series (8086, 80286, 80386, 80486, Pentium, Core i3/i5/i7/i9), AMD Ryzen and Athlon, the ARM processors in nearly every phone and tablet, and Apple Silicon.

short.q: Describe the Impact Printers with the examples.
short.a:
Impact printers form characters by physically striking an inked ribbon against the paper. Because they must strike, they are noisy and comparatively slow, and their quality is limited.

Dot matrix builds each character from a grid of tiny pins. It is cheap to run and can print through carbon paper, which is why it survives wherever multi-part forms are needed.

Daisy wheel has characters moulded on the petals of a wheel, and strikes the right petal. The quality is like a typewriter, but no graphics are possible.

Chain and drum printers are fast line printers once common in data centres.

short.q: Describe Non-Impact Printers with the example.
short.a:
Non-impact printers put the image on the paper without anything striking it, so they are quiet, fast and capable of high quality — but they cannot print through carbon paper.

Inkjet sprays microscopic droplets of ink. Quiet, cheap to buy and excellent for photographs, though ink is expensive and the head can dry out.

Laser draws the image as static charge on a drum with a laser beam, picks up toner with it, and fuses the toner with heat. Fast, sharp and quiet — the standard office printer.

Thermal heats special paper, as in a till receipt; silent and simple, but the print fades and the paper is expensive.

short.q: Write short notes on: a. Mouse b. Keyboard c. MICR d. Joystick e. Scanner f. Light pen g. VDU h. OCR i. Touch Screen j. Plotter l. Cache Memory m. LCD Monitor n. Laser printer o. USB port p PCI slot q. HDMI
short.a:
Mouse — a pointing device whose movement on a surface moves the pointer; it selects and drags in a graphical interface.

Keyboard — the standard device for entering text and commands.

MICR — Magnetic Ink Character Recognition; reads characters printed in magnetic ink, so cheques can be read reliably even when stamped or dirty. Used by banks.

Joystick — a lever reporting direction and tilt; used in games, simulators and for controlling machinery.

Scanner — converts a paper image into a digital image.

Light pen — a photosensitive pen that detects position on a CRT screen, allowing drawing directly on it; now largely historical.

VDU — Visual Display Unit, the screen; the standard soft-copy output device.

OCR — Optical Character Recognition; converts an image of text into editable text.

Touch screen — detects where a finger touches the display, so the display is also the input device.

Plotter — draws with pens on large sheets; the right tool for maps, architectural plans and engineering drawings.

Cache memory — a small, very fast memory holding copies of the data the processor is most likely to need next, so it does not stall waiting for main memory.

LCD monitor — a flat panel controlling light through liquid crystals; thin, light and low-power.

Laser printer — a non-impact printer using a light beam and toner; fast, sharp and quiet.

USB port — Universal Serial Bus; the standard plug-and-play connection for modern peripherals, which also supplies power.

PCI slot — an expansion slot on the motherboard accepting an additional circuit board, such as a sound, network or graphics card.

HDMI — High Definition Multimedia Interface; carries digital audio and video on a single cable.

long.q: Define computer system. Explain the characteristics of a computer.
long.a:
A computer system is the complete working arrangement of hardware, software, data and the people who use it. The hardware is the physical equipment; the software is the set of instructions; the data is what the software works on; and the people supply the purpose. All four must work together, because a failure in any one of them makes the whole system useless.

A computer itself is an electronic device that accepts data, processes it under the control of a stored program, and produces information — automatically, at high speed and with accuracy. Six characteristics define it:

  1. Speed — millions to billions of operations per second, so work that would take a person days finishes in seconds.
  2. Accuracy — results are exact provided the input and the program are correct. This is conditional, not absolute: the machine will repeat a bad instruction perfectly, which is the "garbage in, garbage out" principle.
  3. Diligence — it does not tire, so the ten-thousandth calculation is as careful as the first.
  4. Versatility — the same hardware becomes a typewriter, a cinema or a calculator depending on the program it is given.
  5. Storage — enormous quantities of data can be held and recalled almost instantly.
  6. Automation — once instructed it completes the whole task without further human intervention.

long.q: What are the application areas of the computer? Explain in detail. Discuss how the development of the PCs (Personal Computers) has extended the use of the computer at present days.
long.a:
Computers are applied in nearly every field of work. The main areas are:

  • Education — e-learning, digital libraries, online examination and school administration.
  • Business — accounting, invoicing, payroll, inventory and customer records; spreadsheets make "what if" questions answerable in seconds.
  • Office — word processing, email, scheduling and shared documents.
  • Communication — email, voice and video calls, messaging and social media.
  • Banking — ATMs, online banking, electronic fund transfer and fraud detection.
  • Health and medicine — patient records, CT and MRI imaging, monitoring equipment and research.
  • Industry — automation, robots, process control, CAD and CAM.
  • Military — simulation, logistics, navigation and guidance.
  • Aviation — reservation, air-traffic control, simulation and autopilot.
  • Robotics, graphics, design and research — from exploring other planets to weather forecasting and genetics.

The effect of the personal computer. Before the microprocessor, a computer was a shared, expensive resource kept in a special room and operated by specialists. Putting a whole processor on one chip moved computing onto the desk, and then into the bag and the pocket. Three things followed: the cost fell until a computer became an ordinary household purchase; the interface became graphical, so no programming knowledge was needed to use one; and networking let those cheap machines share data, which produced the internet and everything built on it. Computing stopped being a service that an organisation bought and became something an individual simply does.

long.q: Explain the different generations of computers.
long.a:
A generation marks a change in the underlying switching technology, not a modest improvement. Five are recognised.

First generation (1940–1956) — vacuum tubes. Machines such as ENIAC and UNIVAC-I used tens of thousands of glass valves. They filled rooms, consumed enormous power, failed frequently and were programmed in machine language.

Second generation (1956–1963) — transistors. The transistor was small, solid, cool and dependable. Size and power fell by an order of magnitude, and assembly language and early high-level languages such as FORTRAN and COBOL appeared.

Third generation (1964–1971) — integrated circuits. Many transistors on one chip. Hardware finally became reliable enough to be worth sharing, so operating systems, multiprogramming and terminals appeared (IBM System/360).

Fourth generation (1971–present) — microprocessors. An entire CPU on one chip. This produced the personal computer, graphical interfaces, networks and the internet.

Fifth generation (present and beyond) — artificial intelligence. Defined by capability rather than by components: parallel processing, natural language, machine learning and robotics.

long.q: What do you mean by generation of computer? Explain the technology used in different generations of computers.
long.a:
A generation of computers is a stage in development marked by a fundamental change in the technology used to build the machine — specifically, in the component used for switching and storage of bits. Improvements within one technology make a computer faster or smaller but do not create a new generation.

The technologies, in order, are: vacuum tubes (first), transistors (second), integrated circuits (third), microprocessors (fourth) and artificial intelligence (fifth). Each change brought the same pattern of benefits: smaller size, lower power, greater reliability and lower cost — which is why each generation reached far more users than the one before it.

long.q: What are the different types of computer on the basis of size/speed and working principle? Explain them in brief.
long.a:
By size, speed and capacity:

  • Supercomputer — the fastest and most expensive; thousands of processors in parallel, rated in FLOPS. Used for weather forecasting, nuclear simulation and cryptography.
  • Mainframe — built for enormous input/output volumes and many simultaneous users; the backbone of banks, airlines and government.
  • Minicomputer — mid-range, serving a department or controlling a process; cheaper than a mainframe.
  • Microcomputer — built around one microprocessor; the personal computer.

By working principle:

  • Analog — works on continuously varying physical quantities such as voltage or temperature; it measures rather than counts.
  • Digital — works on discrete binary 0 and 1. Every computer in ordinary use is digital, because digital data can be copied and transmitted without any loss of accuracy.
  • Hybrid — combines both, converting analog signals from the physical world into digital form for processing. Used in intensive-care monitoring and industrial control.

long.q: Explain the different microcomputers which are portable in nature.
long.a:
Portable microcomputers are distinguished mainly by size, weight and how they are carried:

  • Laptop — a complete computer with folding screen, keyboard, battery and pointing device in one unit; the general-purpose portable machine.
  • Notebook — a thinner, lighter laptop, originally the size of a sheet of paper.
  • Tablet — a flat touchscreen device with no physical keyboard, designed around touch and gestures.
  • Palmtop / PDA — small enough to hold in one hand; intended for scheduling and notes, and now largely replaced by the smartphone.
  • Workstation — not portable, but worth contrasting: a high-performance single-user machine for technical or scientific work.

The trade-off is consistent: the smaller the device, the less capable it is for long or heavy work. A phone fits in a pocket but nobody writes a program on one.

long.q: What do you mean by computer architecture? Describe each functional component of computer architecture with the typical diagram.
long.a:
Computer architecture is the design of a computer as the programmer sees it: the instruction set, the data formats, the addressing modes and the registers. (Computer organisation is different — it is how that design is physically built.) Almost every computer follows the von Neumann architecture, whose central idea is the stored program: instructions and data share the same memory.

The five functional units are:

  1. Input unit — accepts data and instructions and converts them to machine-readable form.
  2. Memory unit — holds instructions, data and results.
  3. Arithmetic and Logic Unit — carries out arithmetic and comparisons.
  4. Control unit — fetches, decodes and directs the execution of instructions; it does not process data itself.
  5. Output unit — converts results into a form a person can use.

In the usual block diagram the input unit feeds memory; the control unit reads from memory and drives the ALU; the ALU reads operands from and writes results back to memory; and results pass to the output unit. The control unit and ALU together form the CPU.

long.q: Discuss the term computer architecture. Draw block diagram and explain the main components of a computer system.
long.a:
Computer architecture is the contract between the machine and the programmer — what instructions exist and what they do. Organisation is the engineering that implements it. Two processors can share an architecture while being organised completely differently inside.

The main components of the system, and the direction data flows between them:

  • Input unit — keyboard, mouse, scanner and the rest, converting the outside world into binary.
  • Storage unit — primary memory holding the running program and its data, plus secondary storage for permanent retention.
  • ALU — all arithmetic and all comparisons.
  • Control unit — the director; it fetches each instruction, decodes it and issues the control signals that make the other units act.
  • Output unit — monitor, printer, speakers.

They are connected by three buses: the data bus carries the value, the address bus carries where it is to go, and the control bus carries the timing signals that say when. One instruction cycles through fetch, decode, execute and store.

long.q: Define the term computer peripheral. Discuss the different types of printers with their merits and demerits.
long.a:
A peripheral is any device connected to the computer that is not part of the core processing system — input, output or storage devices attached through a port.

Printers divide first into impact and non-impact:

Impact printers strike an inked ribbon against the paper.

  • Dot matrix — builds characters from a grid of pins. Merits: cheap to run, and can print through carbon paper to make multi-part forms. Demerits: slow, noisy, low quality.
  • Daisy wheel — strikes moulded characters, giving typewriter quality. Merits: excellent text. Demerits: no graphics, slow, noisy.

Non-impact printers do not touch the paper.

  • Inkjet — sprays microscopic ink droplets. Merits: quiet, cheap to buy, superb for photographs. Demerits: ink is expensive and the head can dry out.
  • Laser — a laser draws a charged image on a drum, toner sticks to it, and heat fuses it. Merits: fast, sharp, quiet, economical per page at volume. Demerits: higher purchase price, and colour units are bulky.
  • Thermal — heats special paper, as in a till receipt. Merits: silent and simple. Demerits: the print fades and special paper is needed.

long.q: What are the different types of memories used in a computer system? Explain them in brief.
long.a:
Memory is arranged as a hierarchy — the faster it is, the smaller and more expensive it is.

  • Registers — a handful of storage locations inside the CPU; the fastest and smallest of all.
  • Cache — small, very fast memory holding copies of the data the processor is most likely to need next, so it does not stall waiting for main memory.
  • Primary memory (RAM) — holds the running programs and their data. It is volatile. SRAM (used for cache) needs no refresh; DRAM (used for main memory) must be refreshed constantly.
  • ROM — non-volatile memory holding the startup instructions. PROM is written once, EPROM is erased by ultraviolet light, and EEPROM is erased and rewritten electrically — the basis of flash memory.
  • Secondary storage — hard disks, solid-state drives, optical discs and pen drives. Non-volatile, slower and far cheaper per byte.
  • Tertiary storage — magnetic tape and optical jukeboxes, used for archival backup. Cheapest of all, but sequential access makes it slow.

long.q: Explain the different softcopy output devices.
long.a:
Soft copy is output displayed on a screen rather than printed. It is immediate, editable and searchable, but temporary — it vanishes when the machine is switched off unless it has been saved.

  • CRT monitor — an electron beam scans a phosphor-coated tube. Excellent colour and viewing angle, but deep, heavy and power-hungry.
  • LCD monitor — liquid crystals control light from a backlight. Thin, light and low-power, though contrast can fall off at an angle.
  • LED monitor — an LCD panel with light-emitting-diode backlighting, giving better brightness and contrast.
  • Plasma display — small cells of ionised gas emit light; good for very large screens, now largely superseded.
  • Monochrome and grayscale displays — one colour, or shades of grey; used where colour carries no information.
  • Projector — throws the screen image onto a large surface for teaching or presentation.
  • Speakers and headphones — audio output, and the only sensible choice for sound.

long.q: What is the CPU? Explain the major units of the CPU.
long.a:
The Central Processing Unit is the part of the computer that executes instructions — the component people mean when they say "the computer". It is built from the control unit, the arithmetic and logic unit, and a small set of registers, and on a modern machine all of it sits on one microprocessor chip.

Control unit. It fetches each instruction from memory, decodes it, and issues the control signals that tell the other units what to do. It does not process data itself — it directs everyone else. It uses the program counter to track which instruction comes next.

Arithmetic and Logic Unit (ALU). It performs the actual work: arithmetic (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division) and logical operations (comparisons, AND, OR, NOT). Results are held in the accumulator.

Registers. A handful of very fast storage locations that hold the instruction being worked on, the data it needs and its result — the program counter, the instruction register, the memory data register and the accumulator among them.

These units are linked internally and to memory by buses, and their speed is set by the clock. A 3 GHz clock steps the processor three thousand million times a second.

blocks.text: A number system is a way of writing quantities using a fixed set of symbols. The system you use every day is decimal; the one a computer uses is binary. Understanding why, and being able to convert between them by hand, is the whole of this chapter — and it is examined directly, so the methods matter more than the definitions.
The number of distinct digit symbols a system uses. It is also the value each position is multiplied by as you move left. Decimal has base 10, binary base 2, octal base 8, hexadecimal base 16.

Every positional number system works the same way: the value of a number is the sum of each digit multiplied by the base raised to the power of that digit's position, counting from zero at the right of the point. Once that one sentence is understood, all four systems are the same idea with a different base.
Why 452 in decimal means what it does: 4×10² + 5×10¹ + 2×10⁰ = 400 + 50 + 2 = 452. The same number written 452₈ would mean 4×8² + 5×8¹ + 2×8⁰ = 256 + 40 + 2 = 298 in decimal.

sections.title: Types of Number System and Conversion

blocks.text: Four systems are used in computing. Each exists because it solves a particular problem that the others handle badly.

head: System
Base
Digits used
Why it is used
rows: What people use. The input and output form.
What the hardware uses — a wire is either on or off.
A compact way to write binary: each octal digit is exactly three bits.
The compact form in real use: each hex digit is exactly four bits.

blocks.text: The binary number system

Binary uses only 0 and 1 because the physical components inside a computer are two-state devices: a transistor conducts or it does not, a voltage is high or low, a magnetic domain points one way or the other. There is no reliable way to build a ten-state switch, so base 2 is not a preference — it is a consequence of the physics.
One binary digit — a single 0 or 1.

Because binary is so long-winded (the decimal number 255 is 11111111 in binary), octal and hexadecimal exist purely as shorthand. Both are powers of two, so converting between them and binary can be done by grouping bits — no arithmetic at all.
Conversions
Any base to decimal — multiply and add
Multiply each digit by the base raised to its position, then add. This works for every base and is the method to fall back on when you cannot remember a shortcut.
Convert (1101)₂ to decimal. 1×2³ + 1×2² + 0×2¹ + 1×2⁰ = 8 + 4 + 0 + 1 = 13.
Convert (2A7)₁₆ to decimal. 2×16² + 10×16¹ + 7×16⁰ = 512 + 160 + 7 = 679. (A is 10 in decimal.)

Convert (110.101)₂ to decimal. Whole part: 1×2² + 1×2¹ + 0×2⁰ = 6. Fractional part uses negative powers: 1×2⁻¹ + 0×2⁻² + 1×2⁻³ = 0.5 + 0 + 0.125 = 0.625. So the value is 6.625. Note that the fractional part alone is 0.625 — a common exam question asks for just that.
Decimal to any base — divide and collect the remainders

blocks.title: Repeated division
items: Divide the number by the target base.
Write down the remainder — it is the next digit, starting from the right.
Divide the quotient by the base again.
Repeat until the quotient is zero.
Read the remainders from the last one back to the first.

blocks.text: Convert (52)₁₀ to binary. 52÷2 = 26 r0; 26÷2 = 13 r0; 13÷2 = 6 r1; 6÷2 = 3 r0; 3÷2 = 1 r1; 1÷2 = 0 r1. Reading the remainders upward: 110100.
Convert (25)₁₀ to octal. 25÷8 = 3 r1; 3÷8 = 0 r3. Reading upward: 31₈. Check: 3×8 + 1 = 25.
Decimal fractions — multiply and collect the whole parts

blocks.title: Repeated multiplication
items: Multiply the fraction by the target base.
The whole-number part of the result is the next digit, going right from the point.
Keep only the fractional part and multiply again.
Stop when the fraction becomes zero or when you have enough digits.

blocks.text: Convert 0.625 to binary. 0.625×2 = 1.25 → take 1, keep 0.25; 0.25×2 = 0.5 → take 0, keep 0.5; 0.5×2 = 1.0 → take 1, keep 0. So 0.625 = 0.101₂.
Binary to octal and hexadecimal — group the bits
This is the shortcut worth memorising, because it needs no arithmetic at all.

items: Binary → octal: split the bits into groups of three starting from the right, and write each group as one octal digit.
Binary → hexadecimal: split into groups of four from the right, and write each group as one hex digit.
Pad the leftmost group with zeros if it is short.

blocks.text: Convert (11010110)₂ to octal. Group in threes from the right: 011 | 010 | 110 → 3 | 2 | 6 → (326)₈.
Convert the same byte to hexadecimal. Group in fours: 1101 | 0110 → D | 6 → (D6)₁₆.
Convert (C3)₁₆ to binary. C = 1100 and 3 = 0011, so the answer is 11000011. This is the quickest way to do it — never go via decimal.

Have students convert the same number three ways — via division, via grouping — and confirm they agree. Then time them on a byte. The grouping method is so much faster that they will remember why it exists.
Binary arithmetic follows exactly the rules you already use in decimal, except that you carry at 2 instead of at 10.
Binary addition

items: 1 + 1 = 0, carry 1
1 + 1 + 1 = 1, carry 1 (when a carry comes in)

blocks.text: Add 1011 and 0110. Working right to left: 1+0 = 1; 1+1 = 0 carry 1; 0+1+carry1 = 0 carry 1; 1+0+carry1 = 0 carry 1. The final carry becomes a new leading digit: 10001. Check in decimal: 11 + 6 = 17, and 10001₂ = 17.
Binary subtraction

items: 0 − 1 = 1, borrow 1 from the next column to the left

blocks.text: Subtract 0101 from 1101. Right to left: 1−1 = 0; 0−1 needs a borrow → 1, borrow from the next column; the next column becomes 0 after lending, so 0−0 = 0; 1−0 = 1. Result 1000. Check: 13 − 5 = 8, and 1000₂ = 8.
Binary multiplication and division

Multiplication is the same long-multiplication method as decimal, and it is trivial because the only multiplier digits are 0 and 1 — each partial row is either zero or a shifted copy of the multiplicand. Division is repeated subtraction with shifting, exactly as in decimal long division.
Multiply 101 by 11. 101 × 1 = 101; 101 × 1 shifted one place = 1010. Adding: 101 + 1010 = 1111. Check: 5 × 3 = 15, and 1111₂ = 15.
Representing negative numbers: complements
Subtraction in hardware is expensive, so computers do not subtract — they add the negative of a number. To do that, a negative number has to be representable, and the method used is the complement.
Formed by inverting every bit — every 0 becomes 1 and every 1 becomes 0.
Formed by taking the one's complement and adding 1. It is the representation actually used in computers, because it gives a single unambiguous zero and makes subtraction a matter of addition.

blocks.title: Two's complement of a binary number
items: Start with the binary form of the positive value.
Invert every bit to get the one's complement.
Add 1 to the result.

blocks.text: Find the two's complement of 0100 (decimal 4). Invert: 1011. Add 1: 1100. So −4 is represented as 1100 in four bits.
Find the one's complement of 1001. Invert every bit: 0110.

blocks.title: Why two's complement and not one's?
blocks.text: In one's complement, zero has two representations — 0000 and 1111 — which makes comparison circuitry awkward. In two's complement there is exactly one zero, and the same adder hardware handles both addition and subtraction. That is why every real processor uses it.

Subtract 2 from 5 using two's complement. 5 = 0101, 2 = 0010. Two's complement of 0010: invert to 1101, add 1 → 1110. Now add: 0101 + 1110 = 10011. Discard the carry out of the leftmost bit, leaving 0011 = 3. Correct: 5 − 2 = 3.
Do the 5 − 2 example on the board twice: once by borrowing, once by adding the two's complement. Students generally trust it only after seeing the discarded carry explained.

Everything in this half of the chapter rests on a single observation: the statements you make about the real world are either true or false, and there is no third option. That is what makes it possible to build reasoning out of switches.

The algebra of logic, in which variables take only two values — true (1) and false (0) — and the operations are AND, OR and NOT. Named after George Boole, who published it in 1854, a century before it was applied to circuits.

Its importance in computing was recognised by Claude Shannon in 1937, who showed that Boolean algebra could describe switching circuits. From that point, circuit design stopped being guesswork and became algebra.

sections.title: Boolean Values, Expressions and Truth Tables

blocks.text: One of exactly two values: true or false, written as 1 or 0.
A symbol that stands for a Boolean value — A, B, X, Y by convention.
A combination of Boolean variables, constants and operators that evaluates to true or false. For example A + B′C.
A Boolean expression together with the rule that gives its output for each combination of inputs — that is, an expression viewed as a mapping from inputs to one output.
The three basic operators
Note that OR in Boolean algebra is inclusive: A + B is true when both are true. The everyday "either/or" is exclusive-OR, which is written separately as A ⊕ B.
Truth tables
A table listing every possible combination of inputs to a Boolean expression and the resulting output. With n inputs there are 2ⁿ rows.
A truth table is the definition of an operation: two expressions are equal if and only if their truth tables are identical. That single rule is how the laws below are verified.
An electronic circuit that takes one or more binary inputs and produces a single binary output according to a Boolean operation. Gates are the physical form of Boolean algebra.
Seven gates are studied. Three are basic, two are universal, and two are exclusive. Learning them as three families is far easier than learning seven unrelated symbols.
Basic gates

head: Gate
Boolean function
Truth table (A, B → Y)
Behaviour in one line
rows: Output is high only when every input is high.
Output is high when any input is high.

blocks.text: Universal gates
A gate from which any Boolean function can be built using only copies of itself. NAND and NOR are universal, which is why real chips are largely made of them.

head: Gate
Boolean function
Truth table (A, B → Y)
Behaviour in one line
rows: The opposite of AND: low only when both inputs are high.
The opposite of OR: high only when both inputs are low.

blocks.title: Why "universal" matters
blocks.text: Because any circuit can be built from NAND gates alone, a manufacturer can mass-produce one gate type and construct everything from it. An AND gate is a NAND followed by a NOT; an OR gate is three NANDs. This is an economic fact about chip fabrication as much as a logical one.
Exclusive gates

head: Gate
Boolean function
Truth table (A, B → Y)
Behaviour in one line
rows: High when the inputs are the same — the equality test.

blocks.text: XOR is the gate that compares. Two bits are equal if their XNOR is 1, and different if their XOR is 1. That is why XOR appears in adders (it produces the sum bit) and in parity checking.

Give each student two cards marked 0 and 1 and have the class act as each gate in turn, holding up the output for every input combination. It turns the truth table from something to memorise into something they have done.
The laws of Boolean algebra let you replace a complicated expression with a simpler one that behaves identically. Fewer terms means fewer gates, which means a cheaper, faster, cooler circuit.
De Morgan's theorems
These two are the most useful and the most often misapplied, so they are worth stating in words as well as symbols.

items: First theorem: the complement of a sum equals the product of the complements — (A + B)′ = A′ · B′.
Second theorem: the complement of a product equals the sum of the complements — (A · B)′ = A′ + B′.

blocks.text: In words: to negate a compound expression, negate every variable and swap AND with OR. Break the bar, change the sign — that is the whole rule.
Simplify A · (A + B). By the absorption law this is simply A. Verify: A·(A+B) = A·A + A·B = A + A·B (idempotent) = A·(1 + B) = A·1 = A.
Simplify (A + C′)(B′ + C′). Expand: A·B′ + A·C′ + B′·C′ + C′·C′. The last term is C′ by idempotence. Collecting C′ terms: A·B′ + C′(A + B′ + 1) = A·B′ + C′·1 = A·B′ + C′.

sections.title: Verification of Laws using Truth Tables

blocks.text: Any law can be verified by building a truth table for the left-hand side and the right-hand side and confirming that the two output columns are identical. This is not a heuristic — it is a proof, because a Boolean function is completely defined by its truth table.
Verify De Morgan's first theorem: (A + B)′ = A′ · B′.
The column for (A + B)′ and the column for A′ · B′ are identical in all four rows, so the theorem is verified.
Verify the absorption law A + (A · B) = A.
The last two columns match, which confirms the law. Notice that B has no effect on the result at all — that is precisely what "absorption" means.
Standard forms
An expression written as ORs of ANDed terms — for example Y = AB + BC + AC. Each product term is a combination of inputs that makes the output true.
An expression written as ANDs of ORed terms — for example Y = (A + B)(B + C).

Any Boolean function can be written in either form, and the choice is an engineering one: SOP is what you get directly from a truth table by collecting the rows where the output is 1, and it maps naturally onto an AND–OR circuit.
Build the truth table once for De Morgan's theorem and then leave it on the board. Whenever a student is unsure about a simplification later, send them back to that table rather than to the rule.

short.q: Define the base or radix of a number system. Convert (11011.011)₂ into a decimal number.
short.a:
The base (or radix) of a number system is the number of distinct digit symbols it uses, and therefore the factor by which the value of a position changes as you move one place to the left. Decimal has base 10, binary 2, octal 8 and hexadecimal 16.

Convert (11011.011)₂ to decimal. Whole part: 1×2⁴ + 1×2³ + 0×2² + 1×2¹ + 1×2⁰ = 16 + 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 27. Fractional part: 0×2⁻¹ + 1×2⁻² + 1×2⁻³ = 0 + 0.25 + 0.125 = 0.375. So (11011.011)₂ = 27.375.

short.q: What is the binary number system? Convert (520)₁₀ into base 16.
short.a:
The binary number system is a base-2 system using only the two digits 0 and 1. Computers use it because their basic components are two-state devices — a switch is on or off, a voltage is high or low — so base 2 is the only base the hardware can represent directly and reliably.

Convert (520)₁₀ to hexadecimal. Divide repeatedly by 16: 520 ÷ 16 = 32 remainder 8; 32 ÷ 16 = 2 remainder 0; 2 ÷ 16 = 0 remainder 2. Reading the remainders upward gives (208)₁₆. Check: 2×16² + 0×16 + 8 = 512 + 8 = 520.

short.q: Convert (110111101)₂ binary number into an octal number.
short.a:
Group the bits into threes starting from the right, padding on the left if needed: 110 | 111 | 101. Each group is one octal digit: 110₂ = 6, 111₂ = 7, 101₂ = 5. So (110111101)₂ = (675)₈.

Check in decimal: (110111101)₂ = 445, and (675)₈ = 445.

short.q: Why is the binary number system important in digital computers?
short.a: Three reasons, in order of importance. First, physical: the building blocks of a computer are two-state devices, so base 2 is the only base that maps directly onto the hardware without an unreliable intermediate representation. Second, reliability: distinguishing two levels (high and low voltage) leaves a wide margin for noise, so binary signals survive transmission and copying almost perfectly — which is why digital audio and video do not degrade the way analog tape does. Third, logic: with only two values, the rules of Boolean algebra apply directly, so arithmetic and decision-making can both be built from the same simple gates.

short.q: What is a number system? Convert (567)₈ octal into a hexadecimal number.
short.a:
A number system is a notation for representing quantities using a fixed set of symbols, where the position of each symbol determines the value it contributes. The number of symbols is the base of the system.

Convert (567)₈ to hexadecimal. The quick route is through binary. Each octal digit becomes three bits: 5 = 101, 6 = 110, 7 = 111, giving 101110111. Now group into fours from the right, padding on the left: 0001 | 0111 | 0111, which is 1 | 7 | 7. So (567)₈ = (177)₁₆.

Check in decimal: (567)₈ = 375, and (177)₁₆ = 375.

short.q: What is the binary number? Convert (111111)₂ binary number into an octal number.
short.a:
A binary number is a number expressed in base 2, written using only the digits 0 and 1. Each position represents a power of 2 rather than a power of 10.

Convert (111111)₂ to octal. Group in threes from the right: 111 | 111. Each group is 7, so (111111)₂ = (77)₈.

Check: (111111)₂ = 32 + 16 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 63, and (77)₈ = 63.

short.q: What is the octal number system? Convert (356)₁₀ into base 8.
short.a:
The octal number system is base 8, using the digits 0 to 7. It is used in computing as a compact way to write binary: because 8 = 2³, each octal digit stands for exactly three bits, so conversion is a matter of grouping rather than arithmetic.

Convert (356)₁₀ to octal. 356 ÷ 8 = 44 remainder 4; 44 ÷ 8 = 5 remainder 4; 5 ÷ 8 = 0 remainder 5. Reading upward: (544)₈.

Check: 5×8² + 4×8 + 4 = 320 + 32 + 4 = 356.

short.q: What is the octal number system? Convert (456)₈ octal into a base 2 number system.
short.a:
The octal system is base 8, using digits 0–7, and each octal digit corresponds to three binary digits.

Convert (456)₈ to binary. Write each digit as three bits: 4 = 100, 5 = 101, 6 = 110. Joining them gives 100101110₂.

short.q: Convert 333 denary into a hexadecimal number and back to the base two number system.
short.a:
"Denary" is another name for the decimal system, base 10.

333 to hexadecimal. 333 ÷ 16 = 20 remainder 13 (which is D); 20 ÷ 16 = 1 remainder 4; 1 ÷ 16 = 0 remainder 1. Reading upward: (14D)₁₆.

Back to binary. Write each hex digit as four bits: 1 = 0001, 4 = 0100, D = 1101, giving 101001101₂ (leading zeros may be dropped).

Check: (14D)₁₆ = 1×256 + 4×16 + 13 = 256 + 64 + 13 = 333.

short.q: What is the octal number system? Convert (BAC)₁₆ hexadecimal into a binary number system.
short.a:
The octal system is base 8, digits 0–7, with each digit representing three bits.

Convert (BAC)₁₆ to binary. Each hex digit is four bits: B = 1011, A = 1010, C = 1100. Joining them gives 101110101100₂.

short.q: What is a logic gate? Explain the AND, OR and NOT gates with their truth tables.
short.a:
A logic gate is an electronic circuit that takes one or more binary inputs and produces a single binary output according to a Boolean operation. Gates are the physical form of Boolean algebra and the building blocks of every digital circuit.

AND gate — output is high only when every input is high. Y = A·B: 00→0, 01→0, 10→0, 11→1.

OR gate — output is high when any input is high. Y = A + B: 00→0, 01→1, 10→1, 11→1.

NOT gate — inverts its single input. Y = A′: 0→1, 1→0. It is sometimes called an inverter.

short.q: What are universal gates? Why are NAND and NOR called universal gates?
short.a:
Universal gates are gates from which any Boolean function — and therefore any digital circuit — can be constructed using only copies of that one gate type. NAND and NOR are the two universal gates.

NAND is universal because a NAND with its inputs tied together acts as a NOT, a NAND followed by that NOT gives AND, and three NANDs produce OR. Since AND, OR and NOT together can express any Boolean function, NAND alone can too. The argument for NOR is the mirror image of it.

This matters practically: a manufacturer can mass-produce a single gate type and build everything from it, which is why most real chips are largely made of NAND.

short.a:
First theorem: the complement of a sum equals the product of the complements — (A + B)′ = A′ · B′.

Second theorem: the complement of a product equals the sum of the complements — (A · B)′ = A′ + B′.

short.q: Explain one's and two's complement with examples.
short.a:
One's complement is formed by inverting every bit: every 0 becomes 1 and every 1 becomes 0. The one's complement of 1001 is 0110.

Two's complement is formed by taking the one's complement and adding 1. The two's complement of 0100 (decimal 4) is 1011 + 1 = 1100, so 1100 represents −4 in four bits.

Why two's complement is preferred. In one's complement, zero has two representations (0000 and 1111), which complicates comparison. Two's complement has exactly one zero, and it lets the same adder hardware perform subtraction: to compute 5 − 2, add 0101 to the two's complement of 0010 (which is 1110), giving 10011; discard the carry out of the leftmost bit and the result is 0011 = 3.

short.q: What is a truth table? Give the truth table for a two-input XOR gate.
short.a:
A truth table lists every possible combination of inputs to a Boolean expression together with the resulting output. With n inputs there are 2ⁿ rows. It is a complete definition of the function: two expressions are equal if and only if their truth tables match.

long.q: What is the number system? Explain the different number systems.
long.a:
A number system is a way of writing numbers using a fixed set of symbols. Two things define one: the base (or radix), which is how many digits it has, and the place value of each position, which is a power of the base.

The base is everything. In base b, the rightmost digit counts units, the next counts bs, the next b2s, and so on. Change the base and the same digit string means a completely different quantity — 10 is ten in decimal, two in binary, and sixteen in hexadecimal.

The four systems used in computing

SystemBaseDigitsWhy it is used
Decimal100–9What people use. It has no special role in a computer.
Binary20, 1What the computer actually uses: two symbols map directly onto a switch being off or on, which is reliable to build and to read.
Octal80–7A shorthand for binary. One octal digit is exactly three bits, so conversion is grouping, not arithmetic.
Hexadecimal160–9, A–FThe standard shorthand. One hex digit is exactly four bits, so a byte is two hex digits — which is why memory addresses and colours are written in hex.

The general rule for reading any number is the same. For (dn…d1d0)b the value is Σ di × bi. Applying it to (1011)2 gives 1×23 + 0×22 + 1×21 + 1×20 = 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11.

Converting between them

To decimal — expand by place value, as above.

From decimal (integer part) — divide repeatedly by the target base and read the remainders in reverse. Converting 25 to binary: 25÷2 = 12 r 1, 12÷2 = 6 r 0, 6÷2 = 3 r 0, 3÷2 = 1 r 1, 1÷2 = 0 r 1; read upwards, 11001.

From decimal (fractional part) — multiply repeatedly by the target base and take the whole-number parts in order. Converting 0.625: 0.625×2 = 1.25 → 1, 0.25×2 = 0.5 → 0, 0.5×2 = 1.0 → 1, giving .101. So 25.625 = 11001.101.

Binary ↔ octal and hex — group the bits, three at a time for octal, four at a time for hexadecimal, working outwards from the point in both directions. No arithmetic at all, which is precisely why these bases are used.

long.q: Explain the complement of a number along with the complements of the binary and decimal number systems. Why is the complement method important for a computer system?
long.a:
The complement of a number is what must be added to it to reach a fixed reference value. Complements exist because they let subtraction be carried out with the machinery of addition, and that is the whole reason they matter.

Decimal complements

For an n-digit decimal number N:

The (r−1)’s complement, more simply the 9’s complement, is (10n − 1) − N — subtract each digit from 9. For N = 4567: 9999 − 4567 = 5432.

The r’s complement, the 10’s complement, is 10n − N, which is just the 9’s complement plus 1. For N = 4567: 5432 + 1 = 5433.

Binary complements

Exactly the same idea in base 2. For an n-bit number N:

1’s complement = (2n − 1) − N, obtained by inverting every bit. For N = 10110: 01001.

2’s complement = 2n − N, obtained by inverting every bit and adding 1. For N = 10110: 01001 + 1 = 01010.

A short cut for the 2’s complement that avoids the two-step: copy the bits from the right up to and including the first 1, then invert everything to its left. For 10110 the first 1 from the right is the second bit, so copy 10 and invert 101 to 010, giving 01010.

Why it matters

Because it removes the need for subtraction hardware. To compute A − B, form the complement of B and add. If the addition produces a carry out of the top bit, discard it; if it does not, the result is negative and is itself in complement form.

That single fact has three large consequences.

First, the machine needs only an adder. Subtraction, and therefore comparison, come free.

Second, signed numbers get a representation for nothing. In 2’s complement the top bit serves as the sign, there is only one zero — whereas 1’s complement has a positive and a negative zero — and the range is asymmetric, running from −2n−1 to +2n−1 − 1 for n bits.

Third, arithmetic is uniform: the same adder handles signed and unsigned operands, with no special cases. This is why every processor in ordinary use stores integers in 2’s complement.

Worked example — 7 − 5 in 4-bit 2’s complement. 7 is 0111; 5 is 0101, whose 2’s complement is 1011. Adding: 0111 + 1011 = 10010. Discard the carry, leaving 0010 = 2. Correct.

The correspondence is exact: AND is the intersection of two sets, OR is their union, NOT is the complement. That is not a coincidence or a memory aid — Boolean algebra and set theory have the same structure.

detailed.heading: Chapter 3 — Computer Software and Operating System
detailed.note: Detailed teaching notes written from the Class 11 textbook, illustrated with the screenshots printed in the book. Every topic is explained so that a lesson can be taught without the physical book.
learning_objectives: Define software and distinguish it from hardware.
Classify software into its categories and give examples of each.
Explain what an operating system is and the two roles it plays.
List and explain the functions of an operating system.
Distinguish multiprogramming, multitasking, multiprocessing and distributed systems.
Describe the features of a GUI operating system using Windows as the example.
Work confidently with the Windows desktop, windows and File Explorer.
Customise the desktop, manage devices and use the Control Panel and system tools.
