blocks.text: Hardware on its own does nothing useful. A machine with a processor, memory and a disk but no programs is inert — it can execute instructions, but nobody has given it any. Software is the set of those instructions, and it is the part of the system that actually decides what the machine is for.
A collection of programs, procedures and related data that tell the computer hardware what to do. Unlike hardware, it cannot be touched — it has no physical form of its own.

The relationship is worth stating plainly: hardware is the body, software is the mind. Neither is useful alone, and the interesting work happens at the boundary where the operating system meets the machine.
Software versus hardware

head: Aspect
Hardware
Software
rows: Contains defects ("bugs") that must be corrected

blocks.text: Software is grouped by what it does for the user. The two broadest groups are system software, which runs the machine, and application software, which does the user's actual work.

head: Category
Purpose
Examples
rows: Runs and manages the computer itself
Performs a specific task for the user
Runs in a browser, hosted remotely

blocks.text: System software

System software exists to make the hardware usable — by the user and, more importantly, by other software. It includes the operating system itself, the device drivers that let the OS talk to particular pieces of hardware, the language translators that turn source code into machine code, and the utility programs that keep the system healthy.
Application software

Application software is what most people mean by "a program". It is written to do a job the user cares about. The distinction from system software is one of purpose, not of quality or complexity: the operating system exists to serve the applications, and the applications exist to serve the user.

items: General-purpose — usable across many fields: word processors, spreadsheets, presentation tools.
Specific-purpose (bespoke) — written for one job: payroll, hotel booking, school administration.
Packaged (off the shelf) — bought ready-made and used as supplied.
Customised — a package adapted for a particular organisation.

blocks.text: Utility software

Utility software sits between the two: it does not do the user's work, but it keeps the machine able to do it. Antivirus scanning, disk defragmentation, file compression, backup and system monitoring all belong here.

blocks.title: Firmware, revisited
blocks.text: Some software is fixed permanently into a chip so that it survives switching off — the startup code of a PC, for example. That is firmware, and it is the reason a computer can begin working at all before the operating system has been loaded from disk.

sections.title: Concept and Role of the Operating System

blocks.text: System software that manages the computer's hardware and software resources and provides the services that programs need. It is the layer between the hardware and everything else.

Without an operating system, every program would have to contain its own code for reading the disk, drawing on the screen and talking to the keyboard — and only one program could run at a time. The OS removes that burden and makes the machine shareable.

blocks.caption: Basic organisation of an operating system — the OS sits between the hardware and the applications

blocks.text: The role of the operating system
The operating system plays two roles that pull in opposite directions, and much of its design is the tension between them.

items: As an extended machine. It presents a simpler, cleaner interface than the raw hardware — files instead of disk sectors, windows instead of a memory buffer. Programmers work with an abstraction, not with the machine.

As a resource manager. It decides which program gets the processor, which gets memory, and which gets the disk or the printer when several want them at once. It allocates fairly, prevents interference, and keeps the whole system running.

blocks.text: A useful way to say it: the OS makes the machine easier to use from above, and possible to share from within.
Why an operating system is needed

items: To start the computer and load other programs.
To provide a way for the user to interact with it — a command line or a graphical interface.
To let several programs run and share memory, the processor and peripherals without interfering.
To organise files on disk so that data can be found again.
To control who may use the machine and what they may reach.
To handle errors — a failing disk, a printer out of paper — without crashing everything.

blocks.text: The functions below are what an operating system is actually doing at any moment. Exam questions often ask for "the functions of an operating system", and this list is the answer.

head: Function
What it involves
rows: Creating and ending processes, scheduling which runs, pausing and resuming them, and letting them communicate.
Allocating memory to each program, keeping them out of each other's space, and reclaiming it when they finish.
Organising files into directories, controlling who may read or change them, and mapping logical files onto physical disk blocks.
Driving peripherals through device drivers, buffering data, and sharing devices among programs.
Authenticating users, enforcing permissions, and isolating programs from one another.
Providing the command line or graphical desktop through which a person operates the machine.
Tracking resource use for billing or for performance monitoring.
Detecting and reporting faults in the processor, memory, disk or peripherals without losing the whole system.

blocks.text: Process management and scheduling
A program in execution — the program code together with its current state: the values in its registers, its memory and the files it has open.
The policy the operating system uses to decide which ready process gets the processor next, and for how long.
Scheduling exists because there are always more runnable processes than processors. The aim is to keep the processor busy, be fair, and respond quickly to whatever the user is doing.
Memory management

items: Keeping track of which parts of memory are in use and by whom.
Deciding which processes to load when there is not enough room for all of them.
Allocating and reclaiming memory as processes start and finish.
Protecting one process's memory from another — a fault in one program must not corrupt its neighbour.

blocks.text: Four words describe how an operating system handles more than one task at a time. They are routinely confused, and the differences are exactly what is examined.

head: Term
Meaning
The key distinction
rows: Several programs are held in memory at once, and the processor switches to another whenever the running one waits for input or output.
The goal is to keep the processor busy; there may be only one processor.
The user works with several programs at the same time, each in its own window or session.
This is multiprogramming with rapid switching, so the user perceives concurrency.
Two or more physical processors work on parts of a task together.
This is genuinely simultaneous — it needs more than one processor.
Several independent computers cooperate over a network and appear to the user as one system.
The work is spread across separate machines.

blocks.title: The distinction that matters
blocks.text: Multiprogramming and multitasking can both run on a single processor — they create the appearance of doing several things at once by switching rapidly. Multiprocessing cannot: it requires more than one processor and is genuinely parallel. If a question asks which needs multiple processors, the answer is multiprocessing.
Other terms
Jobs are collected into groups and run one after another without user interaction — efficient for payroll and billing, where nothing depends on a human answering.
The system must respond within a guaranteed time limit. Used where a late answer is a wrong answer: aircraft control, intensive-care monitoring, industrial robots.
Many users share one computer, each getting a slice of processor time in turn, fast enough that each feels they have the machine alone.
A small program that lets the operating system communicate with one specific piece of hardware — a printer, a graphics card, a scanner. Without the right driver the device does nothing.

Booting is the process of starting the computer: firmware runs first, checks the hardware, then finds and loads the operating system from disk into memory. Only once that is done can anything else run.

A GUI (graphical user interface) replaces typed commands with visual objects — windows, icons, menus and a pointer. Windows is the most familiar example, and its features are the ones exam questions ask about.

blocks.caption: A typical Windows desktop

blocks.text: Features of a GUI operating system

items: Windows — each program runs in its own rectangular area, which can be moved, resized, minimised or closed.
Icons — small pictures standing for programs, files and folders.
Menus — lists of commands, so the user chooses rather than recalls.
Pointer — a mouse or touchpad controls a cursor that selects and drags.
WYSIWYG — what you see on screen is what you get on paper, which is why the GUI transformed desktop publishing.
Multitasking — several programs visible and running at once.

blocks.text: The trade-off against a command-line interface is real: a GUI is easier to learn and far less intimidating, but it consumes more memory and processor time, and for repetitive work a typed command is often faster than a series of clicks.

blocks.caption: The Windows environment — the onscreen work area

sections.title: Working in the Desktop and Window Environment

blocks.text: The desktop and its parts

head: Element
What it does
rows: The working background; the surface on which everything else sits.
A bar, usually at the bottom, showing running programs and giving quick access to others.
The main route to programs, settings, files and power options.
Shortcuts to programs, files, folders and drives.
Clock, volume, network status and background-program icons.
Minimise, maximise/restore and close, at the top right of each window.

blocks.text: Working with windows

blocks.title: Common window operations
items: Open a window by double-clicking its icon or a file.
Move it by dragging the title bar.
Resize it by dragging any edge or corner.
Switch between open windows from the taskbar, or with Alt+Tab.
Arrange windows side by side by snapping one to each half of the screen.
Close with the close button, or with Alt+F4.

blocks.text: Running a program

blocks.title: Three ways to start an application
items: Click its icon on the desktop, if it has one.
Open the Start menu, find the program and click it.
Open the file you want to work on — Windows starts the program that owns that file type.

sections.title: Managing Files and Folders with File Explorer

blocks.text: File Explorer is the Windows tool for managing files and folders. Everything below is done in it, and these are the operations the book illustrates step by step.

blocks.caption: From File Explorer, double-click a folder to open it

blocks.text: Files and folders
A named collection of data stored on disk — a document, a program, a photograph. The name usually ends in an extension such as .docx or .jpg that identifies the type.
A named container holding files and other folders, used to keep the disk organised. Folders can be nested to any depth.
Core operations

blocks.title: Create a folder
items: Open the location where the folder should go.
Right-click empty space, choose New, then Folder.
Type the name for the folder and press Enter.

blocks.caption: A new folder is created
Type the name for the new folder

blocks.title: Move a file or folder
items: Select the item.
Drag it to the destination folder and release the mouse button.
The item appears in the new location. The same technique moves a whole folder, together with everything inside it.

blocks.caption: Dragging a file into its new location
The same technique moves an entire folder

blocks.title: Rename a file or folder
items: Right-click the item and choose Rename.
Type the new name and press Enter.

blocks.caption: Right-click and choose Rename

blocks.title: Delete a file or folder
items: Select the item and press Delete, or right-click and choose Delete.
The item moves to the Recycle Bin — it is not gone yet.
To remove it permanently, right-click the Recycle Bin and choose Empty Recycle Bin.

blocks.caption: Deleting a file or folder
Emptying the Recycle Bin deletes items permanently

blocks.title: Deleting a folder
blocks.text: Deleting a folder deletes every file inside it as well. Windows will normally warn you first — read the warning before confirming, because restoring from the Recycle Bin is much easier than recovering a file that has been emptied from it.
Selecting files

items: One file — click it.
A group — click the first file, hold Shift, click the last; everything between is selected.
Scattered files — hold Ctrl and click each one.
Everything — press Ctrl+A, or choose Select all from the menu.

Selecting a group of files

blocks.text: Do the whole create–rename–move–delete cycle live on a projector, ending with emptying the Recycle Bin. Students who watch the Recycle Bin save an accidental deletion will remember to check it.

sections.title: Customising Windows, Devices and System Tools

blocks.text: Customising the desktop

items: Change the background — right-click the desktop, choose Personalise, then pick a picture, a solid colour or a slideshow.
Change the theme — a theme sets the background, window colours, sounds and screen saver together.
Change the resolution — higher resolution shows more, but makes text and icons smaller.
Pin programs — pin frequently used programs to the taskbar or the Start menu so they are always one click away.

blocks.caption: Display settings

blocks.text: The Control Panel

The Control Panel is the traditional place to change how Windows behaves — hardware, accounts, programs, appearance and network settings. Modern Windows moves many of these into the Settings app, but the Control Panel remains the fuller view.

blocks.caption: Programs available from the Control Panel

blocks.text: Installing and removing devices

blocks.title: Attaching a new device
items: Connect the device; Windows detects it and installs a driver automatically in most cases.
If it does not, install the driver supplied by the manufacturer.
Check in Device Manager that the device appears without a warning mark.
To remove it, use the safely-remove option for external drives so that nothing is left half-written.

blocks.text: Passwords and privacy

items: Use a strong, unique password for each account and change it if you suspect it is known.
Set a screen lock so an unattended machine cannot be used.
Review which apps may reach your camera, microphone and location, and withdraw permission where it is not needed.
Keep the system updated — updates close the holes that malware uses.

blocks.text: System tools and accessories

head: Tool
Used for
rows: Removing temporary and unneeded files to free space.
Reorganising fragmented data so the disk reads faster.
Seeing what is running, and ending a program that has stopped responding.
Viewing hardware and updating or removing drivers.
Making copies of files that can be recovered after a failure.
The small accessories supplied with Windows.

sections.title: Open Source and Mobile Operating Systems

blocks.text: Software whose source code is published under a licence that lets anyone read, modify and redistribute it — usually freely, and usually with the condition that modifications are shared on the same terms.

The distinction is about licence, not price. Open-source software is usually free of charge, but the defining feature is that you receive the source code and the right to change it. "Freeware" is free to use but closed; "open source" is open whether or not money changes hands.

head: Aspect
Open source
Proprietary
rows: Community and forums; paid support available
Can be adapted to local needs
Fixed; you get what is supplied

blocks.text: Linux and UNIX
A portable, multi-user, multitasking operating system developed at Bell Labs from 1969. Its design — small tools, plain-text files, everything-is-a-file — shaped most later systems.
A free, open-source, UNIX-like operating system kernel created by Linus Torvalds in 1991 and now maintained by developers worldwide.

Strictly, Linux is the kernel — the core that manages the hardware. What people call "Linux" is that kernel plus the GNU tools, a desktop environment and applications. That combination is why the whole system is sometimes called GNU/Linux.

head: Feature
UNIX
Linux
rows: Still used in servers and workstations
Dominates servers, supercomputers, Android and embedded systems

blocks.text: Linux distributions
A complete operating system built around the Linux kernel — kernel plus system tools, a package manager, a desktop environment and applications, assembled and maintained as one product.

head: Distribution
Aimed at
Notes
rows: The most widely used desktop distribution; easy to install.
Stability above all; the base for many others including Ubuntu.
Sponsored by Red Hat; showcases newer technology.
Built on the Linux kernel, but not a desktop Linux in the usual sense.

blocks.text: Mobile operating systems
An operating system designed for phones, tablets and wearables — built for touch input, wireless networking, low power use and a small screen.

head: System
Maker
Notes
rows: Based on the Linux kernel; the most widely used mobile OS in the world.
Runs only on Apple hardware; known for a tightly controlled app store.
iOS adapted for larger tablet screens.
For feature phones with limited hardware.

blocks.text: Earlier mobile systems worth naming in an exam: Symbian (dominant before smartphones), Windows Phone (discontinued), BlackBerry OS (once standard in business) and Palm OS.

If a spare machine or a virtual machine is available, boot a live Ubuntu USB in class. Five minutes of clicking through a Linux desktop settles more questions about open source than any comparison table.

short.q: Define software. What are the categories of software?
short.a:
Software is a collection of programs, procedures and related data that tell the computer hardware what to do. It has no physical form of its own — it is the instructions, not the machine.

The categories are: system software, which runs and manages the computer (operating systems, device drivers, language translators); application software, which does the user's work (word processors, spreadsheets, browsers); utility software, which maintains the system (antivirus, backup, disk cleanup); web-based software, which runs in a browser from a remote server (Gmail, Google Docs); and mobile apps, built for phones and tablets.

short.q: What is an operating system? Explain the functions of an operating system.
short.a:
An operating system is system software that manages the computer's hardware and software resources and provides the services programs need. It is the layer between the hardware and everything else.

Its functions are: process management (creating, scheduling and ending processes); memory management (allocating and protecting memory); file management (organising files and directories, controlling access); device management (driving peripherals through drivers); security and protection (authenticating users, enforcing permissions); providing the user interface; job accounting; and error handling.

short.q: Differentiate between multiprogramming, multitasking and multiprocessing.
short.a:
Multiprogramming keeps several programs in memory at once, and the processor switches to another whenever the running one waits for input or output. The aim is to keep the processor busy. It needs only one processor.

Multitasking is multiprogramming with switching fast enough that the user perceives several programs running at once, each in its own window. It also needs only one processor.

Multiprocessing uses two or more physical processors working at the same time. This is genuinely parallel and requires more than one processor.

The distinction exam questions look for: multiprogramming and multitasking create the appearance of concurrency on one processor; multiprocessing is real concurrency on several.

short.q: What is a device driver and why is it needed?
short.a:
A device driver is a program that lets the operating system communicate with one specific piece of hardware — a printer, a graphics card, a scanner.

It is needed because the operating system cannot know about every device that exists, and should not have to: the OS defines a standard interface, and each manufacturer supplies a driver that translates standard requests into the commands that particular device understands. Without the correct driver, the hardware is connected but useless.

short.q: What is open-source software? Give examples.
short.a:
Open-source software is software published under a licence that lets anyone read, modify and redistribute the source code, usually free of charge and usually on condition that changes are shared on the same terms.

The defining feature is the licence and access to the source — not the price. Freeware is free but closed; open source is open whether or not money changes hands.

Examples: Linux, the Apache web server, Firefox, LibreOffice, and the Android Open Source Project.

short.q: What is Linux? What is a Linux distribution?
short.a:
Linux is a free, open-source, UNIX-like operating system kernel created by Linus Torvalds in 1991. Strictly it is only the core that manages the hardware; what people call Linux is that kernel plus the GNU system tools, a desktop environment and applications — which is why the whole system is sometimes called GNU/Linux.

A distribution (distro) is a complete operating system assembled around the Linux kernel: kernel, system tools, a package manager, a desktop environment and applications, maintained together as one product. Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora, Linux Mint and Red Hat Enterprise Linux are distributions; Android is also built on the Linux kernel.

short.q: Explain the features of a GUI operating system.
short.a:
A graphical user interface replaces typed commands with visual objects. Its features are windows (each program in its own area, movable and resizable), icons (pictures standing for programs, files and folders), menus (so the user chooses rather than recalls), a pointer controlled by mouse or touchpad, WYSIWYG output (what you see is what you get), and multitasking (several programs visible at once).

The trade-off: a GUI is easier to learn and less intimidating than a command line, but it uses more memory and processor time, and for repetitive work a typed command is often faster.

short.q: How do you manage files and folders using File Explorer?
short.a:
File Explorer is the Windows tool for organising files. The operations are:

  • Create a folder — right-click empty space, choose New then Folder, type the name and press Enter.
  • Move — drag the item to the destination folder and release. The same technique moves a whole folder with everything in it.
  • Rename — right-click, choose Rename, type the new name and press Enter.
  • Delete — select and press Delete, or right-click and choose Delete. The item goes to the Recycle Bin, from which it can be restored; emptying the Recycle Bin removes it permanently.
  • Select — click for one file, Shift-click for a range, Ctrl-click for scattered files, Ctrl+A for everything.

short.q: What is booting?
short.a:
Booting is the process of starting the computer. Firmware runs first and checks the hardware, then locates the operating system on disk and loads it into memory. Only after that has happened can any other program run.

A cold boot starts from a machine that was switched off; a warm boot restarts one that was already running.

short.q: Differentiate between system software and application software.
short.a:
System software runs and manages the computer itself. It exists to make the hardware usable — by the user and by other software. Examples: the operating system, device drivers, language translators, and utility programs.

Application software performs a specific task that the user cares about. Examples: a word processor, a spreadsheet, a browser, a game.

The distinction is one of purpose, not of complexity: the system software exists to serve the applications, and the applications exist to serve the user.

long.q: Explain the functions of an operating system in detail.
long.a:
An operating system is system software that manages the computer's hardware and software resources. It plays two roles: from above it presents an extended machine — a simpler, cleaner interface than the raw hardware, with files instead of disk sectors and windows instead of memory buffers; from within it acts as a resource manager, deciding which program gets the processor, memory and peripherals, and keeping them from interfering with each other.

Its functions in detail:

  • Process management — creating and ending processes, scheduling which one runs, pausing and resuming them, and letting them communicate safely.
  • Memory management — allocating memory to each program, keeping them out of one another's space, and reclaiming memory when a program finishes.
  • File management — organising files into directories, controlling who may read or change them, and mapping logical files onto physical disk blocks.
  • Device management — driving peripherals through device drivers, buffering data, and sharing devices among competing programs.
  • Security and protection — authenticating users, enforcing permissions and isolating programs from one another.
  • User interface — providing the command line or graphical desktop through which a person operates the machine.
  • Job accounting and error handling — tracking resource use, and detecting and reporting faults so that one failure does not bring down the whole system.

long.q: Describe the different types of operating systems with examples.
long.a:
Batch operating system. Jobs are collected into batches and run one after another with no user interaction. Efficient for payroll and billing, where nothing depends on a person answering. Example: early mainframe systems.

Multiprogramming operating system. Several programs are held in memory at once, and the processor switches to another whenever the running one waits for input or output, so the processor is never idle.

Multitasking (time-sharing) operating system. Switching is fast enough that each user perceives the machine as their own. Example: Windows, Linux, macOS.

Multiprocessing operating system. Two or more physical processors work together on a task. Example: server editions of Linux and Windows Server.

Real-time operating system. Must respond within a guaranteed time limit, because a late answer is a wrong answer. Example: aircraft control, intensive-care monitoring, industrial robots.

Distributed operating system. Several independent computers cooperate over a network and appear to the user as one system.

Mobile operating system. Designed for touch input, wireless networking, low power and a small screen. Examples: Android, iOS.

A collection of related application programs sold and installed as one unit, designed to share data and a common interface.

The alternative is a set of unrelated standalone tools. The package wins because the learning transfers — once you know where the menus are in one program of the suite, you can find your way around the others — and because data moves between them without exporting and importing.

Predicting the weather from measured data

sections.title: The Six Domain-Specific Systems in Detail

blocks.text: School management system

A school runs on records: who is enrolled, who attended, who sits which exam, who has paid. Holding these in separate paper registers means the same information is written several times and disagrees with itself. A school management system holds it once.

items: Admission and student records — enrolment, personal details, class allocation.
Attendance — daily records per class, withabsence reports for parents.
Timetable — allocating teachers, rooms and periods without clashes.
Examination and results — entering marks, calculating grades, printing report cards.
Fees — billing, receipts and outstanding balances.
Library and transport — often included in the same system.

blocks.text: The benefit is that the report card is produced from the same marks that were entered once, so there is no re-typing and no version of the truth to reconcile.
Inventory management system

Stock is money sitting on a shelf. Too little and sales are lost; too much and cash is tied up. An inventory system keeps track so that reordering happens at the right moment rather than by guesswork.

items: Records every item, its quantity and where it is held.
Raises a purchase order when stock falls to a set reorder level.
Tracks suppliers, prices and delivery times.
Values the stock on hand at any date.
Reports slow-moving and obsolete items, so they can be cleared.

blocks.text: Payroll system

Payroll turns attendance and salary rules into the correct amount of money for each person, every month, together with the deductions and records the law requires. It is the application where an error is least forgivable.

items: Employee master — name, post, grade, bank details, tax status.
Attendance and leave — days worked, overtime, leave taken.
Earnings — basic salary plus allowances.
Deductions — tax, provident fund, insurance, loans.
Output — payslips, bank transfer lists, and statutory returns.

blocks.text: Financial accounting system

Whereas payroll is about one calculation done for many people, an accounting system is about recording every transaction and then summarising it. The flow is always the same: transactions are entered as vouchers, posted to ledgers, and summarised into the financial statements.

items: Voucher entry — each transaction recorded once, with the accounts it affects.
Ledger — all transactions for one account, in date order.
Trial balance — a check that debits and credits are equal.
Profit and loss — income minus expenses over a period.
Balance sheet — what the organisation owns and owes on one date.

blocks.text: Hotel management system
A hotel sells the same room repeatedly, so its central problem is knowing what is free, for which nights, at what price — and charging correctly for everything the guest used.

items: Reservation — booking rooms for dates, with availability and rates.
Front desk — check-in, room allocation, check-out.
Billing — room charges plus restaurant, laundry and other services, on one folio.
Housekeeping — which rooms are clean, occupied or needing service.
Reporting — occupancy rates and revenue per available room.

blocks.text: Weather forecasting system
Weather forecasting is the most technical application in the chapter, and the one where the computer is not merely keeping records but doing original work: solving the equations of the atmosphere.

items: Data collection — temperature, pressure, humidity and wind from ground stations, balloons, ships and buoys.
Satellite and radar — cloud images and precipitation over a wide area.
Numerical models — supercomputers solve the physical equations forward in time to predict the state of the atmosphere.
Forecast output — maps and bulletins for the public, and warnings for severe weather.

blocks.text: Because the atmosphere is chaotic, small errors in the starting data grow, which is why forecasts are given as probabilities and why accuracy falls off sharply beyond a few days.

Ask students to name one piece of software used at home — a school portal, a shop bill, a bus ticket. Mapping each back to one of the six systems shows that "domain-specific" describes software they already meet.

mcq.q: MS-Word is an example of ......... software.
mcq.teacher_note: Word processing is an application package: it does a job for the user. System software runs the machine (Windows, device drivers); utility software maintains it (antivirus, disk cleanup).

mcq.q: What is the default file extension for all Word documents?
mcq.teacher_note: Since Word 2007 the default is .docx — the "x" marking the XML-based format. The older binary format was .doc.

mcq.q: How many ways you can save a document?
mcq.teacher_note: The three routes are the Save button on the Quick Access Toolbar, File > Save, and the shortcut Ctrl + S. Note that Save overwrites the existing file; to keep the original as well you need Save As.

mcq.q: Ctrl + Z is the keyboard shortcut for
mcq.teacher_note: Ctrl + Z is undo. Ctrl + Y (or Ctrl + Shift + Z) is redo, Ctrl + V is paste. Undo is worth memorising: it is the key you reach for whenever something goes wrong.

mcq.q: The word wrap feature
options: Automatically move text to the next line
Appears at the bottom of the document
Allows you to type over text
mcq.teacher_note: Word wrap moves a word down to the next line when it will not fit, so you type continuously and press Enter only at the end of a paragraph.

mcq.q: What does Ctrl + = key effect in MS Word?
mcq.teacher_note: Ctrl + = gives subscript (H2O). Superscript, the raised character (x2), needs Ctrl + Shift + = — the next question. The two are easy to confuse; the extra Shift is what raises the text.

mcq.q: How can you make the selected character superscripted
mcq.teacher_note: Ctrl + Shift + =. Pairs with the previous question: Ctrl + = alone is subscript.

mcq.q: When typing in a word field manually, what must you press to insert the code’s braces?
mcq.teacher_note: Ctrl + F9 inserts the field braces { }. Remember that these braces cannot be typed from the keyboard — they belong to the field, not to the text.

mcq.q: How many different documents you can open at one time?
options: As many as your computer memory will hold
As many as your taskbar can display
mcq.teacher_note: The limit is memory, which is why it has no fixed number. The taskbar and the "no more than three" option describe what you can conveniently see, which is a different question.

mcq.q: Ctrl + B
mcq.teacher_note: B for Bold. Its companions are Ctrl + I for italic and Ctrl + U for underline — three keys, three effects, named after the first letter.

mcq.q: What is the default font used in MS Word 2007 document?
mcq.teacher_note: Word 2007 introduced Calibri as the default, replacing Times New Roman. Preeti is a common Nepali font, not a Word default.

mcq.q: Which of the following is not a type of page margin?
mcq.teacher_note: Note — the printed key for this question says (d) Top, which is an error. A page has four margins: top, bottom, left and right. Top is a margin; Center is an alignment, not a margin. The correct answer is (c) Center.

mcq.q: Which would you choose to save a document with a new name?
mcq.teacher_note: Save As is what creates a second copy under a new name. Plain Save (Ctrl + S) overwrites, which would destroy the original.

mcq.q: Spreadsheet package is used to perform ........ operation.
mcq.teacher_note: A spreadsheet is built around calculation — formulas, functions, what-if analysis. Word processing and presentation are the jobs of the other two packages.

mcq.q: .xlsx is extension file name of .......
mcq.teacher_note: .xlsx is Excel, .docx is Word, .pptx is PowerPoint. The trailing "x" means XML-based, introduced with Office 2007.

options: Use =if() function to format the required numbers red
Apply Conditional Formatting command on Format menu
Select the cells that contain number between 0 and 100 then click red color on Text Color tool
mcq.teacher_note: Conditional formatting is the right tool: it colours cells according to a rule, and it keeps working as the numbers change. Hand-colouring the cells would have to be redone every time the data was edited; =IF() returns a value, it does not format.

mcq.q: In excel file, which of the following cannot be a sheet in workbook?
mcq.teacher_note: A workbook holds worksheets, chart sheets and (in older versions) macro sheets. There is no "data sheet" — data lives in a worksheet.

mcq.q: In excel, which of the following is not the correct method of editing the cell content?
mcq.teacher_note: F2, clicking the formula bar and double-clicking the cell all put the cell into edit mode. The Alt key on its own only reveals the ribbon shortcuts.

mcq.q: Which of the following option is not available in Paste Special dialog box?
mcq.teacher_note: Paste Special offers arithmetic operations — Add, Subtract, Multiply, Divide — so you can apply a value to a range without a formula. There is no SQRT operation.

mcq.q: The shortcut key Ctrl+R is used in Excel to
options: Right align the content of cell
Remove the cell contents of selected cells
Fill the selection with active cells to the right
mcq.teacher_note: Ctrl + R is Fill Right — it copies the leftmost cell of the selection across to the right. Its partner is Ctrl + D, Fill Down. A mnemonic: R for right, D for down.

mcq.q: Which area in an excel window allows entering values and formulas?
mcq.teacher_note: The Formula Bar shows and edits the contents of the active cell. It is where you work on a long formula, since the cell itself is too narrow to see it.

mcq.q: .pptx is extension file name of .......
mcq.teacher_note: .pptx is PowerPoint, matching the "p" for presentation.

mcq.q: MS PowerPoint is used to perform ...... operation.
mcq.teacher_note: One package, one job: Word writes, Excel calculates, PowerPoint presents.

mcq.q: Which of the following statements is not true in PowerPoint?
options: You can type text directly into a PowerPoint slide
From Insert menu choose Picture and then File
You can view a PowerPoint presentation in
You can show or hide task pane from View >>
mcq.teacher_note: Text cannot simply be typed anywhere on a slide — it must go into a placeholder or a text box. The other three are all standard operations: inserting a picture, running the slideshow, and toggling the task pane.

mcq.q: To start or open Microsoft PowerPoint application in your computer
options: Click on Start > Programs > All Programs >
Hit Ctrl + R then type ppoint.exe and Enter
Click Start > Run then type powerpnt then Enter
mcq.teacher_note: The Run command is powerpnt, the executable name. Note that the first option is a menu path and the second uses the wrong executable name, so "all of above" cannot be right.

mcq.q: MS PowerPoint presentation is widely used as / for
mcq.teacher_note: All three are genuine uses — which is the point of the question: a presentation package is general-purpose, not tied to one subject.

mcq.q: Which short cut key inserts a new slide in current presentation?
mcq.teacher_note: Ctrl + M inserts a new slide. Ctrl + N creates a new presentation (a different thing entirely) and Ctrl + S saves.

mcq.q: From which menu you can access picture, chart?
mcq.teacher_note: Anything brought into a document — picture, chart, table, video, hyperlink — comes from the Insert tab in all three Office packages.

mcq.q: In a PowerPoint Presentation
options: Sound clips can be inserted but not movie clips
Movie clips can be inserted but not sound clips
Both sound clips and movie clips cannot be inserted
Both sound clips and movie clips can be inserted
mcq.teacher_note: Both are supported, from the Insert tab. This is what makes a presentation multimedia rather than a set of still images.

mcq.q: ....... is not the DBMS software.
mcq.teacher_note: MS Excel is a spreadsheet, not a database management system — it has no tables with enforced relationships, no queries and no referential integrity. Access and Oracle are DBMSs; Visual Basic is a programming language used to build front-ends for them.

mcq.q: Which field type will you select if you need to enter long text in that field?
mcq.teacher_note: The Memo type holds long text — the ordinary Text type is limited to 255 characters.

mcq.q: The extension of database file in MS Access is ...
mcq.teacher_note: .mdb was the Access extension; from Access 2007 it is .accdb. .dbf belongs to dBase.

mcq.q: Which of the following is not a type of MS Access.
mcq.teacher_note: Number, Text and Memo are data types — they describe what a field holds. A form is a database object for entering and viewing data, not a type of data.

mcq.q: Which of the following is not an object of MS Access?
mcq.teacher_note: Tables, Forms, Queries, Reports, Macros and Modules are Access objects. Worksheets belong to Excel, not Access.

mcq.q: Primary key does not accept…
mcq.teacher_note: A primary key must identify a row uniquely, so it cannot be null and it cannot be duplicated. Text and numbers are both perfectly acceptable keys — a student ID is often a number, a catalogue code often text.

mcq.q: Which is not a type of query?
mcq.teacher_note: Select, Update, Append, Delete and Make-Table are all query types. A form is a database object rather than a query; "search" is something you do with a query, not a type of one.

mcq.q: The feature of school management system is…
options: to keep student information and parent access
mcq.teacher_note: A school system covers all of it. That breadth is the point of a domain-specific package: it is written for one kind of organisation and so can cover every part of its work.

mcq.q: Which is not include in inventory management system.
options: paying employment taxes to the government.
mcq.teacher_note: Paying employment taxes is payroll/accounting work, not inventory work. Tracking, forecasting, reporting and alerts all concern stock.

mcq.q: Which is not include in financial accounting system.
options: tracking of the flow of financial data across the
mcq.teacher_note: Booking and reservation belong to a hotel or reservation system, not to financial accounting. The ledger, payables, receivables and the flow of financial data are all accounting.

mcq.q: Which is not a feature of hotel management system.
options: tracking the motion of air and clouds in the
mcq.teacher_note: Tracking air and clouds is weather forecasting — nothing to do with running a hotel. Housekeeping, human resources, customer relationships and banquets all are.

mcq.q: Which is a feature of weather forecasting system.
options: Looking at current weather conditions and
Tracking the motion of air and cloud in the
mcq.teacher_note: Forecasting combines observation of current conditions with tracking how air and cloud are moving — so all the listed items are features.

mcq.q: Which is not a domain-specific tool.
options: School, hotel and payroll management systems.
mcq.teacher_note: Watching TV is not a tool at all — it is an activity. The others are all software packages built for one domain.

short.q: What is an application package? Give examples.
short.a:
An application package is a collection of related application programs sold and installed as one unit, designed to share data and a common interface. Examples: Microsoft Office (Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Access) and LibreOffice (Writer, Calc, Impress, Base).

The advantage over separate programs is that the same menus and shortcuts appear in every component, and data moves between them without exporting and importing.

short.q: What is a word processor? List its main features.
short.a:
A word processor is application software for creating, editing, formatting and printing text documents.

Its features include: entering and editing text; character formatting (font, size, bold, italic, underline, colour); paragraph formatting (alignment, indentation, spacing, bullets and numbering); page setup (margins, orientation, borders); inserting tables, pictures, shapes and SmartArt; spell and grammar checking; mail merge; and printing.

short.q: What is mail merge? Where is it used?
short.a:
Mail merge produces many personalised documents from one template and a list of recipients. The main document holds the text that is the same for everyone; the data source holds what differs — the names and addresses. Merging the two gives one letter per person.

It is used for letters to parents, appointment letters, invoices, address labels, and any other case where the same message goes to many people.

short.q: What is a spreadsheet? What is it used for?
short.a:
A spreadsheet organises data into a grid of rows and columns, where each cell can hold a value, text or a formula that calculates from other cells.

It is used for budgets, accounts, marksheets, stock records, financial analysis and charts. Its defining strength is that a cell can contain a formula, so changing one number updates every result that depends on it.

short.q: Explain relative, absolute and mixed cell references with examples.
short.a:
A relative reference such as A1 shifts when the formula is copied: copy a formula containing =A1 down one row and it becomes =A2. This is what you want when filling a column of similar calculations.

An absolute reference such as $A$1 is fixed and never changes, however far the formula is copied. Use it when every calculation must refer to the same cell — a tax rate or a conversion factor held in one place.

A mixed reference such as $A1 or A$1 fixes either the column or the row and lets the other shift, which is what you need when building a multiplication table.

Worked example. With the tax rate in C1 and prices in B2 downwards, =B2*C1 filled down gives =B3*C2, =B4*C3 — and the answers become wrong because the rate reference moved. Writing =B2*$C$1 keeps the rate fixed for every row.

short.q: What is the difference between a worksheet and a workbook?
short.a:
A worksheet is one page of cells — a single grid. A workbook is the file that contains one or more worksheets.

A new spreadsheet file typically opens with three worksheets, which is useful for keeping related sets of data separate — one sheet per month, for example — while still keeping them in one file.

short.q: Differentiate between sorting and filtering.
short.a:
Sorting rearranges rows into a chosen order — by name alphabetically, by mark highest to lowest. Every row stays present; only the order changes.

Filtering hides the rows that do not meet a condition, leaving the matching rows visible in their original order. Nothing is deleted or reordered.

Neither changes the data itself — both change how it is displayed.

short.q: What is presentation software? What is the difference between animation and transition?
short.a:
Presentation software creates a sequence of slides combining text, images, charts and multimedia, shown to an audience.

Animation is movement applied to objects within one slide — text flying in, a chart building up. Transition is the visual effect used when moving between slides — a fade, a wipe, a push.

The one-line test: animation is inside a slide, transition is between slides.

short.q: How does a database differ from a spreadsheet?
short.a:
A spreadsheet is built for calculating on numbers; a database is built for retrieving records reliably and enforcing structure.

A database can insist that a required field is filled, that a date is a real date, and that an order belongs to a customer who actually exists. A spreadsheet cannot enforce any of that. Once there are many records, several different kinds of thing, or more than one person editing, a database is the right tool.

In a database the data lives in tables; forms are used to enter it, queries to ask questions of it, and reports to print it.

short.q: What is a domain-specific tool? Give examples.
short.a:
Domain-specific software is written for one field of work, with that field's vocabulary, rules and procedures built in, rather than being a general tool the user must adapt.

Examples from this chapter: a school management system (enrolment, attendance, timetable, results, fees), an inventory management system (stock levels and reordering), a payroll system (salaries, deductions, payslips), a financial accounting system (ledgers, trial balance, profit and loss, balance sheet), a hotel management system (reservation, check-in, billing, housekeeping), and a weather forecasting system (data collection, numerical models, forecast output).

long.q: Explain the components of an office package and what each is used for.
long.a:
An office package is a set of related programs sold as one unit and designed to share data. Its four principal components are:

Word processor — produces text documents: letters, reports, books. It handles character, paragraph and page formatting, tables, pictures and mail merge. Example: Microsoft Word.

Spreadsheet — works with numbers. Data is held in a grid of cells, any of which may contain a formula, so that changing one value updates every dependent result. Used for budgets, accounts, marksheets and charts. Example: Microsoft Excel.

Presentation — builds a sequence of slides combining text, images, charts and media, shown to an audience. Supports animation within a slide and transitions between slides. Example: Microsoft PowerPoint.

Database — stores and retrieves structured records, enforcing the rules that keep them consistent. Objects: tables hold the data, forms enter it, queries ask questions of it, reports print it. Example: Microsoft Access.

The value of the package is integration: a chart built in the spreadsheet can be placed in the word-processed report and shown from the presentation, and all three stay linked to the same numbers.

long.q: Describe the six domain-specific systems covered in this chapter.
long.a:
School management system. Holds the whole record of a school in one place: admission and student records, attendance, timetabling, examinations and results, fees, and often library and transport. The benefit is that report cards are produced from marks entered once.

Inventory management system. Tracks stock so that reordering happens at the right moment rather than by guesswork: item quantities, purchase orders, supplier records, reorder-level alerts, stock valuation, and reports on slow-moving items.

Payroll system. Turns attendance and salary rules into the correct payment for each person each month: employee master records, attendance and leave, earnings and allowances, deductions such as tax and provident fund, and outputs — payslips, bank transfer lists and statutory returns.

Financial accounting system. Records every transaction once as a voucher, posts it to the ledgers, and summarises: trial balance to check that debits equal credits, then the profit and loss account for the period and the balance sheet for the date.

Hotel management system. Solves the central problem of selling the same room repeatedly: reservation with availability and rates, check-in and check-out, a single folio billing room and services together, housekeeping status, and occupancy reporting.

Weather forecasting system. The most technical of the six: it collects observations from ground stations, balloons, ships and buoys, adds satellite and radar imagery, runs numerical models on supercomputers to solve the equations of the atmosphere forward in time, and issues forecasts and severe-weather warnings. Because the atmosphere is chaotic, accuracy falls off sharply beyond a few days, which is why forecasts are given as probabilities.

blocks.text: A program is a list of instructions that tells a computer how to carry out a task. Programming is the work of writing those instructions so precisely that a machine which understands nothing can follow them exactly.
A sequence of instructions written in a programming language to perform a specific task.
An artificial language with a defined vocabulary and grammar, used to write instructions a computer can carry out.

The difficulty of programming is not telling the computer what to do — it is telling it completely. A computer does not guess, infer, or fill in what you obviously meant. Every step must be written, in the right order, with nothing assumed. Learning to program is largely learning to notice what you have left out.

blocks.text: Low-level languages (machine and assembly) are close to the hardware; high-level languages are close to the way people think. C is often called a middle-level language because it gives the readable structure of a high-level language while still allowing direct manipulation of memory and hardware.

blocks.title: Compiler or interpreter — the honest comparison
blocks.text: A compiler produces a standalone machine-code file that then runs at full speed, but it reports errors only after translating the whole program. An interpreter stops at the first error, which makes finding mistakes easier, but it re-examines every statement each time the program runs. C is compiled; Python is interpreted.
Errors

Finding and fixing errors is called debugging, and the name has a real origin: a moth trapped in a relay of the Harvard Mark II in 1947. The three kinds of error are worth separating, because they fail in completely different ways.

head: Kind
When it appears
What it means
Example
rows: The code breaks the grammar of the language — the compiler cannot understand it
A missing semicolon or an unmatched brace
The statement is grammatical but meaningless — a rule about meaning is broken
Adding a number to a string; using an undeclared variable
The program is valid but something goes wrong during execution
Dividing by zero; opening a file that does not exist

blocks.text: A fourth category is worth knowing even though it is not a translator error: a logical error. The program compiles, runs and finishes — and gives the wrong answer, because the reasoning behind it was wrong. These are the hardest to find, precisely because nothing complains.

Which error is which? Writing if (x = 5) where you meant if (x == 5) is a logical error: the code is valid C, it runs, and the condition is simply always true. Writing if (x == 5 with no closing parenthesis is a syntax error, and the compiler will refuse to continue.

blocks.text: The three control structures

Every program, in any language, is built from three structures. This is not a stylistic preference — it is a proved result: sequence, selection and iteration are sufficient to express any computation.

items: Sequence — statements executed one after another, in the order written.
Selection — choosing between alternatives according to a condition (if, if-else, switch).
Iteration — repeating a block while a condition holds (for, while, do-while).

blocks.text: Give the class a real task — making a cup of tea — and have them write the algorithm. The results always omit a step ("fill the kettle" is usually missing), which teaches why algorithms must be complete better than any definition.
Computers store only binary, so every character has to be given a numeric code. Three coding schemes matter.

head: Code
How it works
Used for
rows: Each decimal digit is stored in four bits, so 25 is 0010 0101
Calculators and devices that display decimal digits directly
Seven bits per character, giving 128 values; extended to eight bits for 256
The standard for English text; the basis of most file formats
Uses up to 32 bits, allowing well over a million characters
All the world's writing systems; the default on the web

blocks.text: ASCII is worth knowing in outline: the digits 0–9 occupy codes 48–57, the capital letters A–Z occupy 65–90, and the small letters a–z occupy 97–122. The gap of 32 between upper and lower case is what makes case conversion a single arithmetic operation.

Why does this matter? Because "A" and 65 are the same thing to the machine. Adding 32 to the code for "A" gives 97, which is "a". Sorting text, comparing strings and converting case all depend on these code numbers.

C was developed at Bell Laboratories in the early 1970s by Dennis Ritchie, growing out of two earlier languages, BCPL and B. It was created to write the UNIX operating system — and it succeeded so well that it became the standard language for systems programming.
Why C is still important

items: Portability — a C program written carefully compiles on almost any machine.
Efficiency — the generated code is close to what a good assembly programmer would write.
Control — C allows direct manipulation of memory through pointers, which systems work needs.
Influence — C++, Java, C#, JavaScript and Python all borrow their syntax from C.
Moderate size — the language is small enough to learn completely, with only 32 keywords.

blocks.text: This is why C is often described as a middle-level language: it has the structured statements of a high-level language, but it does not hide the machine from you.

A program that runs before the compiler, handling the lines beginning with #. It includes header files and expands macros.

blocks.text: Use #include <stdio.h> for system headers — the compiler searches its own directories. Use #include "myheader.h" for your own headers — the compiler searches the current directory first.
Comments, tokens and identifiers

items: Comments — // to end of line, or /* ... */ across several lines. They are ignored by the compiler and exist for human readers.
Keywords — the 32 reserved words of the language (int, float, if, else, for, while, return). They cannot be used as names.
Identifiers — names you choose for variables and functions. They must begin with a letter or underscore, may contain letters, digits and underscores, and are case-sensitive.
Constants — fixed values: 10, 3.14, 'A', "hello".
Operators — symbols that act on values: + − * / % = == < > && ||.

blocks.text: C is case-sensitive: total, Total and TOTAL are three different names. This is one of the commonest sources of confusion for beginners.
Data types
Type modifiers change the range or sign: short, long, signed and unsigned. Choosing the right type matters because it decides both how much memory is used and what values can be held.
Variables and constants
A named location in memory whose value can change while the program runs. It must be declared with a type before use.
A value that cannot be changed once defined — written with const or #define.

blocks.text: scanf needs to know where to store what it reads, so it is given the address of the variable: scanf("%d", &a). Forgetting the & is one of the most frequent beginner mistakes in C, and it produces a crash rather than a compile error.

Operators

blocks.text: Two distinctions beginners mix up. = assigns, == compares. And i++ uses the value then increments, whereas ++i increments then uses the value.
Type conversion

When an expression mixes types, C promotes the narrower type to the wider one automatically. Integer division, however, truncates: 7 / 2 is 3, not 3.5. To get a decimal result, make one operand a decimal — 7.0 / 2 or (float)7 / 2. This single rule causes a great many wrong answers.
Selection: if, if-else and switch
A switch is clearer than a long if-else chain when you are comparing one value against several fixed constants.

blocks.title: Do not forget break
blocks.text: Without break, execution falls through into the next case and prints several lines instead of one. This is the classic switch mistake — and unlike most mistakes, the program still runs.
Iteration: for, while and do-while
Use for when you know how many times to repeat; use while when you do not; use do-while when the block must run at least once.
Nested loops
A loop inside another loop. The inner loop completes all of its iterations for each single iteration of the outer one.
Arrays
A collection of elements of the same type stored in adjacent memory locations and accessed by an index. In C, indexing starts at 0 — so the first element of a[5] is a[0] and the last is a[4].

Why start at zero? The name of an array is the address of its first element, and a[i] means "the element i places from the start". So a[0] is the start itself. Reading past the last index is a serious error — C does not check, and the program will read whatever memory happens to be there.
Two-dimensional arrays
A two-dimensional array is an array of arrays, best visualised as a grid of rows and columns. It is declared with two sizes and indexed with two subscripts.

short.q: What is a program? What is a programming language?
short.a: A program is a list of instructions that tells a computer how to carry out a task. A programming language is an artificial language with a defined vocabulary and grammar, used to write those instructions.

short.q: Differentiate between a compiler and an interpreter.
short.a:
A compiler translates the entire program into machine code before it runs. Execution is then fast, but errors are reported only after the whole program has been translated.

An interpreter reads and executes one statement at a time. It stops at the first error, which makes mistakes easier to find, but it re-examines every statement each time the program runs, so execution is slower.

short.q: What are the different types of errors in programming?
short.a:
Syntax errors break the grammar of the language, so the program cannot be translated — a missing semicolon, for example.

Semantic errors break a rule of meaning: the statement is grammatical but meaningless, such as using a variable that was never declared.

Runtime errors occur while a valid program is running — dividing by zero, or opening a file that does not exist.

Logical errors are the hardest: the program compiles, runs and finishes, but gives the wrong answer because the reasoning behind it was wrong. Nothing complains.

short.q: What is an algorithm? What are its characteristics?
short.a:
An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure for solving a problem that finishes after a finite number of steps.

Its characteristics: it has a clear input and a defined output; every step is unambiguous; it is finite — it terminates; and it is effective — each step can actually be carried out.

short.q: Explain the three control structures used in programming.
short.a:
Sequence — statements are executed one after another in the order written.

Selection — a condition decides which branch is taken: if, if-else, switch.

Iteration — a block repeats while a condition holds: for, while, do-while.

These three are sufficient to express any computation, which is a proved result rather than a convention.

short.q: What is the difference between = and == in C?
short.a:
= is the assignment operator: it puts the value on the right into the variable on the left. == is the comparison operator: it tests whether two values are equal.

Confusing them is a classic mistake. Writing if (x = 5) assigns 5 to x, and the condition then evaluates to 5, which C treats as true — so the branch is always taken and no error is reported.

short.q: Why does 7 / 2 give 3 in C and not 3.5?
short.a:
Both operands are integers, so C performs integer division, which discards the remainder: 7 / 2 is 3.

To get a decimal result, make at least one operand a floating-point value — write 7.0 / 2, or cast it with (float)7 / 2. The same rule applies to expressions using variables: (float)a / b.

short.q: What is an array? Why does indexing start at zero in C?
short.a:
An array is a collection of elements of the same type, stored in adjacent memory locations and accessed by an index.

Indexing starts at zero because the name of the array is the address of its first element, and a[i] means "the element i places from the start" — so a[0] is that first element. A consequence is that a[5] runs from a[0] to a[4], and reading a[5] is an error that C will not catch.

short.q: What is a string in C? Why must the array be one character larger than the text?
short.a:
In C a string is an array of characters terminated by the null character \0. That terminator is what tells functions such as strlen where the text ends.

Because the terminator occupies one element, an array holding a five-letter word must be declared with six characters: char name[6] holds "Nepal" — five letters plus the null.

short.q: What is the difference between a while loop and a do-while loop?
short.a:
A while loop tests its condition before the body, so the body may never run at all.

A do-while loop tests its condition after the body, so the body always runs at least once. Use it for things like a menu that must be shown before asking whether to repeat.

long.q: Write a C program to check whether a year is a leap year.
long.a:
One correct solution:

#include <stdio.h>

int main()
{
    int year;
    printf("Enter a year: ");
    scanf("%d", &year);

    if ((year % 400 == 0) || (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0))
        printf("%d is a leap year\n", year);
    else
        printf("%d is not a leap year\n", year);

    return 0;
}

Compile and run it with gcc program.c -o program && ./program.

long.q: Write a C program to find the GCD of two numbers.
long.a:
One correct solution:

#include <stdio.h>

int main()
{
    int a, b, temp;
    printf("Enter two numbers: ");
    scanf("%d %d", &a, &b);

    while (b != 0)
    {
        temp = b;
        b = a % b;
        a = temp;
    }
    printf("GCD = %d\n", a);
    return 0;
}

Compile and run it with gcc program.c -o program && ./program.

long.q: Write a C program to display the sum of the series 1 + 2 + ... + n.
long.a:
One correct solution:

#include <stdio.h>

int main()
{
    int n, i, sum = 0;
    printf("Enter n: ");
    scanf("%d", &n);
    for (i = 1; i <= n; i++)
        sum = sum + i;
    printf("Sum = %d\n", sum);
    return 0;
}

Compile and run it with gcc program.c -o program && ./program.

short.q: What is HTML? What is the basic structure of an HTML document?
short.a:
HTML (HyperText Markup Language) is the language that describes the structure and content of a web page. It is a markup language, not a programming language: it says what things are, not what to do.

The basic structure is:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>Page Title</title>
</head>
<body>
    <h1>Heading</h1>
    <p>A paragraph of text.</p>
</body>
</html>

The head holds information about the page and is not displayed; the body holds everything the visitor sees.

short.q: Differentiate between a web browser and a search engine.
short.a:
A web browser is software that retrieves a page and renders it. It displays the page whose address you give it: Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Safari.

A search engine is a service that has indexed the web and returns the pages matching what you describe: Google, Bing, DuckDuckGo.

The browser is a client that shows pages you name; the search engine is an index that finds pages you describe.

short.q: What is the difference between ordered and unordered lists in HTML?
short.a:
An ordered list (<ol>) numbers its items, and its type attribute chooses the numbering: 1, A, a, I or i.

An unordered list (<ul>) bullets its items, with type choosing disc, circle or square.

A third kind, the definition list (<dl>), pairs a term (<dt>) with its description (<dd>).

short.q: Explain the different types of links in HTML.
short.a:
External — a full URL to another site: <a href="https://example.com">.

Internal (relative) — a filename for another page on the same site: <a href="about.html">.

Same page — <a href="#id"> jumps to the element carrying that id, which is how a contents list works.

short.q: What is CSS? Explain the three ways of adding CSS to a page.
short.a:
CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) describes how a page looks — colours, fonts, spacing and layout — keeping appearance separate from content.

Inline — a style attribute on one element. Use only for a single override.

Embedded — a <style> block in the head, for one page that needs its own styles.

External — a separate .css file linked with <link rel="stylesheet">. This is normal practice, because one file can style an entire site and the browser caches it.

short.q: What is the difference between class and id selectors in CSS?
short.a:
An id selector, written #name, applies to exactly one element on the page — the one carrying that id. It is the most specific.

A class selector, written .name, applies to every element carrying that class, so it can be reused.

Because an id is more specific, it beats a class when both apply to the same element.

short.q: What is a domain name? What is web hosting?
short.a:
A domain name is the readable address of a site, such as example.com, which the DNS system translates into the numeric IP address of the server.

Web hosting is the service of storing a site's files on a server connected to the internet so visitors can reach them.

They are separate purchases: you register the name with one company and rent the space from another, then point the name at the space.

short.q: What is HTML5? Give examples of its new elements.
short.a:
HTML5 is the current version of HTML. It added elements that carry meaning rather than being generic containers, and it made audio and video work without a plug-in.

New elements include <audio> and <video> for media, <source> for offering several formats, <track> for subtitles, <embed> for external content, <canvas> for drawing with JavaScript, and <svg> for scalable vector graphics.

blocks.text: A presentation that uses two or more media at the same time, under computer control. The media may be text, graphics, audio, animation, video or data.

The word itself is simply multi + media: several media working together. A book is not multimedia, because it is only text and still images. A film is arguably multimedia, but it is not computer multimedia, because the viewer cannot influence it. The definition has two halves and both matter: several media, and computer control.
Discrete and continuous media
Media fall into two classes, and the distinction is about time, not about format.

head: Class
Media
What defines it
rows: The content does not change with time — you can look at a photograph for as long as you like
The content unfolds over time — meaning is carried by when something happens
blocks.caption: The two classes of media

blocks.text: A genuinely multimedia presentation normally contains one of each. A slide with text and a chart is not really multimedia, because both parts are static; add a narrated animation and it is.
Interactivity — the point of it all

The ultimate purpose of multimedia is interactivity. In the early days computers only computed, and multimedia appeared almost entirely in games. As processors grew more capable, multimedia spread into education, business, medicine and entertainment, and it has changed how people expect to receive information: not as a fixed sequence to sit through, but as material to move through.
Characteristics of a multimedia system

items: Integrated — several media combined into one coherent presentation, not simply placed side by side.
Digital — stored as binary data, so copies are exact and nothing degrades with use.
Interactive — the user chooses what happens next, rather than watching a fixed sequence.
Non-linear — the user can reach the material in any order, following links rather than reading straight through.
Computer-controlled — a computer decides what is presented and when.

blocks.text: There are five components. The book treats them in this order, and it is a sensible one: each builds on the last in complexity.

blocks.caption: The five components of multimedia.

blocks.text: 1. Text

Text may be a word, a line, or a paragraph — the ordinary written word. It is the easiest component to create: any text editor will do, and a word processor will give you control over typeface, size, colour and style. For special effects you need graphics software rather than a word processor.

blocks.title: Exam note
blocks.text: Text is the component most often overlooked in an exam answer, because it seems too obvious to mention. It is also the component that makes material searchable — a picture cannot be searched for a word inside it. That is the point behind the hyperlink question in the exercise.
2. Graphics or image
A graphic is a picture. Unlike text, which has agreed universal codes (ASCII, Unicode), graphics have no single agreed format — hence JPEG, PNG, GIF, BMP and the rest, each with different strengths.

A computer image is made of pixels — dots on the screen. Resolution is the pixel density together with the number of colours used, and it determines both the quality of the image and its file size. Graphics packages such as Adobe Photoshop, Adobe Illustrator and Paint Shop Pro create images and also compress them, so that a file takes less disk space while keeping resolution and colour.
The proverb "a picture is worth a thousand words" is the argument for using graphics at all: some ideas are conveyed far faster as an image than as prose.
3. Audio

Audio is sound audible to the human ear. Multimedia uses several kinds: the human voice, instrumental notes, and natural sound, in any combination that serves the purpose. It is especially important alongside video and animation.

Sound must be converted into digital form to be used by a computer, and converted back to analogue form so that the user can hear it through speakers. Speech is well suited to commentary and help, because it does not obscure what is already on the screen. Music is the most obvious use, and is largely there to set a mood.
4. Video
Video is a sequence of still pictures shown in rapid succession. The computer reads a clip as a series of frames, each slightly different from the one before, and each read as a bitmap image.

At roughly 15 to 25 frames per second the movement looks smooth rather than jerky — below that the eye sees separate pictures. Video generally uses raster graphics, and in practice it also carries an audio track.
5. Animation

Animation is a sequence of still vector images displayed in rapid succession to produce a visual effect. Where video records reality, animation builds it — which is why it is the right tool for explaining something that cannot be filmed: the inside of an engine, the structure of a molecule, a process over a century.
Animation may be two-dimensional or three-dimensional. Software includes Animator Pro, Maya 3D, AutoCAD, 3D Max and Macromedia Flash.

blocks.caption: Where animation is applied.

blocks.text: The film industry uses it heavily: the high-resolution graphics and animation in films such as I, Robot, Terminator and Titanic are what make them spectacular.

blocks.text: 1. Education

Listening to a lecture makes some topics hard to grasp; seeing the same topic presented with image, sound and motion often makes it immediate. E-books, electronic encyclopedias and electronic dictionaries all carry multimedia. Beyond the classroom, medicine uses it for diagnosis, scientific research uses it to make investigations visible, and engineering drawings become far easier to interpret.
2. Entertainment
The entertainment industry was an early and heavy adopter. High-resolution graphics and animation are what make modern films spectacular.

blocks.caption: The film-making industry is the heaviest user of animation.

blocks.text: 3. Web pages
Early web pages were text only and completely static. Multimedia turned them into dynamic, eye-catching sites carrying graphics and animation.
4. Business
Advertising uses multimedia to convince customers about products and services, letting a company demonstrate what it offers instead of merely describing it.
5. Office automation

Meetings, group discussions, conferences and seminars are central to strategic planning, but the participants are often scattered across the country. Video conferencing, audio conferencing and document sharing make that distance irrelevant.
6. Communication
Chatting used to mean text. Today video chat and audio chat are ordinary, and that is entirely a consequence of multimedia.
Advantages

items: It increases learning effectiveness.
It is more appealing than traditional lecture-based methods.
It offers real potential for improving personal communication, education and training.
It reduces training costs — material is produced once and reused.
It is easy to use, needing no programming knowledge from the user.
It provides high-quality video images and audio.

blocks.text: Disadvantages

items: It is expensive — good multimedia takes time and skilled people.
It is not always easy to configure.
It requires special hardware: capable processors, sound and video, storage.
It is not always compatible — files that work on one system may not work on another.

blocks.title: Exam note
blocks.text: The two lists pair up, and the pairing is the useful way to remember them: engaging but expensive, easy to use but not easy to configure, high quality but demanding of hardware, widely reusable but not always compatible.
