short.q: What is multimedia? Explain its application areas.
short.a:
Multimedia is a presentation that uses two or more media at the same time under computer control — text, graphics, audio, animation, video or data. It combines at least one discrete medium with at least one continuous medium, and its purpose is interactivity.

The main application areas are education (e-books, simulations, diagnosis), entertainment (film, games), web pages, business (advertising, product demonstration), office automation (video conferencing, document sharing) and communication (video and audio chat).

short.q: What are the hardware devices required by a PC to make it multimedia capable?
short.a:
An ordinary PC becomes multimedia-capable with the addition of:

A sound card (now built into the motherboard) with speakers or headphones, for audio. A microphone, to record sound. A high-resolution graphics card and monitor, for good images and video. A CD/DVD drive, the traditional way multimedia was distributed. Large storage — a big hard disk, since video and audio files are far larger than text.

For capturing original material rather than playing it back: a webcam, a scanner or digital camera, and a video capture card. A fast processor with plenty of RAM is needed to handle video smoothly, and a network connection for streamed material.

short.q: Explain the different components of multimedia.
short.a:
There are five.

Text — a word, line or paragraph; discrete, and the component that makes material searchable. Graphics or image — pictures made of pixels; discrete; resolution is the pixel density and colour count. Audio — sound: voice, instrumental notes, natural sound; continuous; must be digitised to be used and converted back to analogue to be heard. Video — a sequence of still frames, roughly 15–25 per second, read as bitmaps; continuous. Animation — still vector images shown in rapid succession; continuous; 2-D or 3-D.

short.q: Describe the advantages of multimedia.
short.a: It increases learning effectiveness, because several senses are engaged at once. It is more appealing than a lecture, so people attend longer. It improves communication, education and training. It reduces training costs, since material is produced once and reused any number of times. It is easy to use, needing no programming knowledge. And it provides high-quality video images and audio.

short.q: Describe any five applications of multimedia.
short.a: Education — interactive lessons and simulations that make difficult topics graspable. Entertainment — films and games. Web pages — sites that are dynamic rather than static text. Business — advertising that demonstrates a product instead of describing it. Office automation — video conferencing and document sharing across distance. Communication — video and audio chat.

short.q: What is computer animation? How is it used in the film-making industry?
short.a:
Computer animation is a sequence of still images displayed in rapid succession to produce a visual effect. It may be 2-D or 3-D, and it is produced with software such as Maya 3D, 3D Max, AutoCAD, Animator Pro and Flash.

In film-making it has two uses. It creates what cannot be filmed at all — creatures, worlds, destruction — and it enhances what can, by adding effects to real footage. Films such as Titanic, Terminator and I, Robot depend on it. The reason it is so effective is that moving images dominate human peripheral vision, so animation seizes attention in a way a still frame does not.

short.q: Write short notes on: a. Multimedia in education. b. Business effect of multimedia.
short.a:
Multimedia in education. A lecture heard once is easily lost; the same material presented with image, sound and motion is grasped far more readily. E-books, electronic encyclopedias and dictionaries carry it. Medicine uses it for diagnosis, research uses it to make investigations visible, and engineering drawings become easy to read.

Business effect of multimedia. Advertising can demonstrate a product rather than describe it, which persuades more effectively. Internally, video conferencing and document sharing let meetings happen across distance, cutting travel and delay. Training is delivered once and reused, which is where the cost saving comes from.

long.q: Explain multimedia in detail, describing all five of its components with their characteristics.
long.a:
Definition. Multimedia is a presentation using two or more media at the same time under computer control. Its purpose is interactivity — the user chooses what happens next. It requires at least one discrete and one continuous medium, and it is characterised by being integrated, digital, interactive, non-linear and computer-controlled.

1. Text. A word, a line or a paragraph. Discrete. Created in any text editor or word processor, with control over typeface, size, colour and style; graphics software is needed for special effects. It is the component that makes material searchable, and it is represented in the computer using ASCII or Unicode.

2. Graphics or image. A picture made of pixels. Discrete. There is no single agreed format, unlike text — hence JPEG, PNG, GIF, BMP. Resolution is the pixel density together with the number of colours, and it sets both quality and file size. Created and compressed with packages such as Photoshop, Illustrator and Paint Shop Pro.

3. Audio. Sound audible to the human ear: voice, instrumental notes, natural sound. Continuous. It must be digitised for the computer to use it, and converted back to analogue so the user can hear it through speakers. Speech suits commentary, because it does not obscure what is already on screen; music sets a mood.

4. Video. A sequence of still frames, each read as a bitmap, shown in rapid succession. Continuous. At 15–25 frames per second the movement appears smooth. It uses raster graphics and normally carries an audio track.

5. Animation. Still vector images shown in rapid succession to give a visual effect. Continuous, and either 2-D or 3-D. Where video records reality, animation builds it, which is why it is the right tool for anything that cannot be filmed. Made with Maya 3D, 3D Max, AutoCAD, Animator Pro and Flash.

Conclusion. The components are complementary rather than alternative: text carries precision, graphics carry structure, audio carries mood, and video and animation carry process. Material that uses only one of them is rarely described as multimedia.

long.q: Describe the applications of multimedia and discuss its advantages and disadvantages.
long.a:
Applications. Education — interactive lessons, e-books, medical diagnosis, research visualisation. Entertainment — film, games, effects. Web pages — dynamic rather than static. Business — advertising and demonstration. Office automation — conferencing and shared documents across distance. Communication — video and audio chat.

Advantages. Greater learning effectiveness; more appealing than a lecture; real gains in communication, education and training; reduced training costs, since material is made once and reused; easy to use, with no programming needed; and high-quality video and audio.

Disadvantages. Expensive to produce well; not always easy to configure; needs special hardware — a capable processor, sound and video, and plenty of storage; and not always compatible between systems.

Discussion. The advantages and disadvantages are two sides of the same coin, and it is worth seeing the pairing: multimedia engages because it is rich, and it is expensive and demanding because it is rich. The cost falls as hardware improves and authoring tools get easier, which is why every one of these disadvantages has become less severe over time — but none has disappeared.

blocks.text: Digital society
A digital society is one in which information and communication technologies have been adopted and integrated into everyday life — at home, at work and in government.

Digital innovations are reshaping society, the economy and industry at a scale and speed we have not seen before. Mobile and cloud technologies, big data and the Internet of Things offer opportunities in health, transport, energy, agriculture, manufacturing, retail and public administration. They can improve how a country is governed, by helping policy-makers decide better and by letting citizens take part. The internet has real potential to promote democracy, cultural diversity and human rights such as freedom of expression and freedom of information.
Computer ethics

Computer ethics are the moral rules governing how computers and networks are used. The issues are not new — property, privacy, honesty and harm — but the technology makes each of them easier to breach and harder to detect.

items: Privacy — not collecting, sharing or reading data about people without their knowledge.
Accuracy — not spreading information you have not checked.
Property — not copying software, music or writing that belongs to someone else.
Access — not using your skills to exclude people who lack them.

blocks.text: The digital divide
The digital divide is the gap between those who have access to modern information technology and those who do not — between rich and poor, urban and rural, educated and uneducated.

Its effect on society is to compound existing inequality. As services move online — banking, government, education, employment — people on the wrong side of the divide are not merely less well served; they are excluded. Bridging it is therefore a policy question, not only a technical one.
Privacy and anonymity
Privacy is the right to control information about yourself — who may collect it, and what they may do with it. Anonymity is acting without your identity being known.

They are related but not the same: a bank transaction is private without being anonymous, since the bank knows exactly who you are. Anonymity has genuine value — it lets people report wrongdoing, seek medical advice, or express an unpopular view without fear. It also makes abuse easier, which is why the tension cannot be resolved once and for all.
Network security

Network security takes physical and software measures to protect the networking infrastructure from unauthorised access, misuse, malfunction, modification, destruction or improper disclosure. The aim is a secure platform on which computers, users and programs can do their permitted work.

A network security system relies on layers — monitoring, security software, and secured hardware and appliances working together. The layering matters: any single measure can fail, so several are placed one behind another.
Information security
Protecting information and information systems from unauthorised access, use, disclosure, disruption, modification or destruction.

blocks.title: Exam note
blocks.text: The three aims pull against one another. The tighter you make confidentiality, the more you risk availability — lock a document down hard enough and the person who legitimately needs it at 2 a.m. cannot get it. Security design is the choice of balance, not the maximising of all three.
Security services

The protections a system provides are called security services. They include authentication (establishing who you are), access control (deciding what you may do), confidentiality, integrity, non-repudiation (a sender cannot deny having sent something) and availability.
Encryption
Converting plaintext into ciphertext so that only someone holding the right key can read it. Decryption reverses the process.

blocks.text: In practice the two are combined: asymmetric encryption is used to agree a key safely, and symmetric encryption then carries the bulk of the data, because it is much faster.
Cryptography and message integrity

Cryptography is the field that covers both. Message integrity is the guarantee that a message arrived exactly as it was sent — provided by hashing rather than by encryption, and worth distinguishing from it: encryption hides a message, integrity proves it was not altered.

blocks.text: Criminal activity that involves a computer, a network or the internet — either committed against computers, or using them as the means.

It is also called computer crime. As the computer has become central to commerce, entertainment and government, cyber crime has grown with it. By the 21st century there was hardly a place in the world untouched by it.
Forms of cyber crime

items: Hacking — gaining unauthorised access to a system.
Identity theft — using someone else’s personal details to obtain credit or services.
Phishing — messages imitating a trusted organisation in order to steal credentials.
Credit card fraud — using stolen card details.
Cyber stalking and bullying — harassment carried out online.
Intellectual property theft — copying software, music or writing without permission.
Denial of service — flooding a service so that genuine users cannot reach it.
Distributing illegal material.

blocks.text: Effects on contemporary society

The financial cost runs to enormous sums each year. Beyond money, identity theft can take years to untangle, and a data breach can destroy the trust an organisation depends on. Because the internet crosses borders, the offender is often in a different country from the victim, which makes prosecution difficult — and that jurisdictional gap is itself the reason cyber crime is so persistent.
Malicious software: any software that brings harm to a computer system — disrupting operation, gathering sensitive information, or gaining access to private systems.

Malware may steal protected data, delete documents, or install software the user never approved. It takes partial or full control of the machine to do whatever its creator wants. Most malware needs the user to trigger it: opening an e-mail attachment, or clicking "OK" on a pop-up from a malicious website.

blocks.title: Exam note
blocks.text: Virus versus worm is the comparison examiners return to. A virus needs a host file and a human action; a worm needs neither. That single sentence answers most questions on the topic.
Spam

Spam is unsolicited bulk electronic mail. It is not itself malware, but it is a common way of delivering it, and it costs time and storage. Much of it is phishing — mail imitating a bank or a delivery company, designed to steal credentials.

Complete security is not achievable, and any claim otherwise should be treated with suspicion. What can be done is to reduce exposure, using a defence-in-depth approach — several measures, so that the failure of one does not expose everything.
Organisational measures

items: Develop clear policies and procedures for the business and its employees.
Create an incident-response plan to support those policies.
Document the security measures already in place.
Use two-factor authentication apps or physical security keys, and activate 2FA on every account that offers it.
Verify requests to send money verbally, with the financial manager.
Create an intrusion detection system.

blocks.text: Personal measures

items: Keep the operating system and applications updated — most attacks exploit known faults for which a fix already exists.
Run current antivirus and anti-malware software.
Use strong, unique passwords; a password manager makes this practical.
Treat unexpected links and attachments with suspicion, even when they appear to come from someone you know.
Back up regularly, and keep one backup disconnected, so that ransomware cannot reach it.
Use a firewall; be cautious on public wireless networks.
Install software only from sources you trust.

blocks.title: Exam note
blocks.text: Two-factor authentication is worth emphasising: it means that a stolen password alone is not enough, which defeats the great majority of opportunistic attacks.

blocks.text: Copyright deserves particular attention in a computing course, because it covers computer programs and databases. It arises automatically — there is no need to register it, and no notice needs to be printed.
A mathematical scheme for demonstrating the authenticity of a digital message or document.

A valid digital signature gives the recipient reason to believe three things: that the message was created by a known sender, that the sender cannot deny having sent it, and that the message was not altered in transit. It therefore provides authentication, non-repudiation and integrity.

It uses asymmetric cryptography in reverse to encryption: the sender signs with their private key, and anyone can verify the signature with the matching public key. Only the holder of the private key could have produced the signature, which is what authenticates it; and because the signature depends on the exact content of the document, any change invalidates it.

Digital signatures are used for software distribution, financial transactions, and anywhere forgery or tampering must be detectable. They play the role for electronic documents that a handwritten signature plays for paper ones — and in two respects they do that job better, since they also prove the document was not altered and are far harder to forge.

sections.title: Concept of Cyber Law in Nepal

blocks.text: Legislation governing acceptable behaviour in the use of technology — computer hardware and software, the internet and networks. It is the part of the legal system that deals with the internet, cyberspace and their legal issues.

It covers a broad area, including freedom of expression, access to and use of the internet, and online privacy. Generically it is called the Law of the Internet. In business it protects companies from unlawful access to, and theft of, their intellectual property.
Why it matters

items: It dictates what actions and reactions are lawful in cyberspace.
It gives online transactions a legal basis, so they can be relied on.
It brings online activity within the reach of the law.
It provides penalties, which is what distinguishes a rule from a request.

blocks.text: The position in Nepal

Nepal’s principal statute is the Electronic Transactions Act, 2063 (2006). It gives legal recognition to electronic records and digital signatures, so that an electronic document can carry the same weight as a paper one. It defines offences including unauthorised access to computer systems, damage to computer systems, and publishing illegal material online, and sets penalties of imprisonment and fines. It also provides for the licensing of certification authorities, which issue digital certificates.

An umbrella term covering all technical means of processing and communicating information — computing, telecommunications, and the content carried on them.

ICT is one of the most powerful and cost-effective tools available for improving public service delivery and government-to-government communication. It can be applied in business, education, health and public administration, letting public officials, businesses and citizens work together to make services more efficient and to strengthen social networks.
What an ICT policy is for

items: Infrastructure — extending networks and connectivity, particularly beyond the cities, which is what narrows the digital divide.
Education — building the skills to use the technology and to produce with it, not only to consume.
E-government — putting public services online so they are reachable and auditable.
Legal framework — the cyber law and regulations that make electronic transactions reliable.
Industry — supporting a domestic technology sector so the country produces as well as buys.
Access and equity — so that the benefits reach those least likely to receive them unaided.

blocks.text: ICT and society

The social impact of ICT is double-edged and is best understood that way. It improves access to education, health information and government; it creates employment; and it connects people across distance. At the same time it widens the gap for those without access, creates new forms of crime, threatens privacy, and can displace work. The purpose of policy is to enlarge the first set of effects and limit the second.

mcq.teacher_note: A firewall is a defence, not a threat. The other three are all malware. Questions of this shape are common: pick the odd one out, and check which way the oddness runs.

mcq.teacher_note: Authentication — establishing who a user is — is a security service, one of the protections a system provides. The other three are attacks or nuisances.

short.q: What do you mean by information security? Explain.
short.a:
Information security protects information and information systems from unauthorised access, use, disclosure, disruption, modification or destruction.

It has three aims, known as CIA: confidentiality (only authorised people can see it), integrity (it has not been altered without authority) and availability (it is there when needed). These pull against one another — tighten confidentiality and you risk availability — so security design is the choice of a balance rather than the maximising of all three.

short.q: Explain the terms of software piracy, plagiarism, and pornography.
short.a:
Software piracy is copying or distributing software without the licence-holder’s permission. It is theft of intellectual property: it takes the creator’s income.

Plagiarism is presenting someone else’s work or ideas as your own. It is dishonesty, and it deprives the original author of credit.

Pornography is material intended to arouse. It raises questions of harm and consent; where it involves minors or is otherwise illegal it is a criminal matter, not merely an ethical one.

short.q: What do you mean by the digital divide? What is its effect on modern society?
short.a:
The digital divide is the gap between people who have access to modern information technology and people who do not — between rich and poor, urban and rural, educated and uneducated.

Its effect is to compound existing inequality. As banking, government, education and employment move online, those on the wrong side of the divide are not merely less well served; they are excluded. That makes bridging it a matter of policy, not only of technology.

short.q: Describe computer ethics in detail.
short.a:
Computer ethics are the moral rules governing how computers and networks are used. The underlying issues are old — property, privacy, honesty and harm — but technology makes each easier to breach and harder to detect.

The main areas are privacy (not collecting or sharing data about people without their knowledge), accuracy (not spreading information you have not checked), property (not copying software, music or writing that belongs to someone else) and access (not using your skills to exclude those who lack them).

short.q: What is an intellectual property right? Explain the types of intellectual property rights.
short.a:
Intellectual property rights are the rights given to people over the creations of their minds. They usually give the creator an exclusive right over the use of the creation for a certain period, and they work like any other property right: the creator is entitled to benefit from their own work or investment.

The types are copyright (original literary and artistic works, including computer programs and databases — arising automatically on creation), patent (inventions), trademark (names, logos and slogans identifying a business) and trade secret (confidential business information, protected by keeping it secret).

short.q: Explain the terms of privacy and anonymity in detail.
short.a:
Privacy is the right to control information about yourself — who may collect it and what they may do with it. Anonymity is acting without your identity being known.

They are related but distinct: a bank transaction is private without being anonymous, because the bank knows exactly who you are. Anonymity has real value — it lets people report wrongdoing, seek medical advice, or express an unpopular view without fear. It also makes abuse easier. That tension cannot be settled once and for all, which is why it keeps reappearing in policy debates.

short.q: Define computer crime and its different forms.
short.a:
Computer crime — another name for cyber crime — is criminal activity that involves a computer, a network or the internet, either committed against computers or using them as the means.

The forms include hacking (unauthorised access), identity theft, phishing, credit card fraud, cyber stalking and bullying, intellectual property theft, denial of service, and distributing illegal material.

short.q: What is cyber crime? Explain its effects in contemporary society.
short.a:
Cyber crime is criminal activity involving a computer, network or the internet. As computers became central to commerce, entertainment and government, it grew with them; by the 21st century hardly any place in the world was untouched by it.

The effects: the financial cost is enormous. Identity theft can take an individual years to untangle. A breach can destroy the trust an organisation depends on. And because the internet crosses borders, offender and victim are often in different countries, which makes prosecution difficult — that jurisdictional gap is a large part of why cyber crime persists.

short.q: Write a short note on the ICT policy of Nepal.
short.a:
ICT — Information and Communication Technology — covers all technical means of processing and communicating information.

An ICT policy directs how a country develops and uses it. Its concerns are infrastructure (extending connectivity, particularly beyond the cities, which narrows the digital divide); education (building skills to produce with technology, not only consume it); e-government (putting public services online so they are reachable and auditable); the legal framework (cyber law, so electronic transactions can be relied on); industry (supporting a domestic technology sector); and access and equity.

short.q: What is a computer virus? How is it transferred from one computer to another? What can be the preventive methods for making a computer safe from viruses?
short.a:
A computer virus is malware that attaches itself to a host file and needs that file to be run in order to spread.

It is transferred through shared or downloaded files — an e-mail attachment, an infected program, a file from an infected pen drive. It cannot travel on its own; some human action is always required.

Prevention. Keep the operating system and applications updated, since most attacks exploit known faults with fixes already available. Run current antivirus software and keep its definitions updated. Do not open unexpected attachments or click unexpected links, even from someone you know. Scan removable media before use. Back up regularly, keeping one backup disconnected so it cannot be encrypted. Install software only from sources you trust.

short.q: What is malicious software? Explain some common malware.
short.a:
Malware is any software that brings harm to a computer system — disrupting operation, gathering sensitive information, or gaining access to private systems. It may steal data, delete documents, or install software the user never approved. Most malware requires the user to trigger it.

A virus attaches to a host file and needs a human action. A worm spreads across the network by itself, needing neither. A Trojan is disguised as something legitimate and does not replicate. Spyware watches and reports rather than destroying. Ransomware encrypts your files and demands payment for the key.

short.q: Explain information security in detail.
short.a:
Information security protects information and information systems from unauthorised access, use, disclosure, disruption, modification or destruction. Network security is the corresponding discipline applied to the networking infrastructure, and it relies on layers of protection, so that the failure of one measure does not expose everything.

The three aims are confidentiality, integrity and availability. Security services — what the system actually provides — include authentication, access control, confidentiality, integrity, non-repudiation and availability.

The mechanisms include encryption (symmetric for bulk data, asymmetric for exchanging keys and for signatures), hashing for message integrity, and digital signatures for authentication and non-repudiation.

short.q: Write short notes on: a. The social impact of ICT. b. Computer crime. c. Cyber law. d. Malware. e. Digital signature.
short.a:
Social impact of ICT. Two-edged. It improves access to education, health information and government, creates employment and connects people across distance; but it also widens the gap for those without access, creates new forms of crime, threatens privacy and can displace work.

Computer crime. Criminal activity involving a computer or network: hacking, identity theft, phishing, card fraud, stalking, IP theft and denial of service.

Cyber law. Legislation governing behaviour in cyberspace; in Nepal the Electronic Transactions Act, 2063 (2006), which recognises electronic records and digital signatures and defines offences with penalties.

Malware. Software that harms a system: viruses, worms, Trojans, spyware, ransomware.

Digital signature. A cryptographic value proving who sent a document and that it was not altered; signed with the sender’s private key, verified with their public key.

long.q: Explain information security in detail: its aims, the security services a system provides, and the role of encryption.
long.a:
Definition. Information security protects information and information systems from unauthorised access, use, disclosure, disruption, modification or destruction. Network security applies the same discipline to the networking infrastructure, and rests on layers of protection — monitoring, security software, and secured hardware and appliances — so that no single failure exposes everything.

The three aims (CIA). Confidentiality — only authorised people can see the information. Integrity — it has not been altered without authority. Availability — it is there when needed. They pull against one another: the tighter the confidentiality, the more availability is at risk. Security design is the choice of a balance, not the maximising of all three.

Security services. What a system actually provides: authentication (establishing who a user is), access control (what they may do), confidentiality, integrity, non-repudiation (a sender cannot deny having sent something) and availability.

Encryption. Plaintext is converted to ciphertext so only the key-holder can read it. Symmetric encryption uses one key for both operations: fast, but the key must be shared safely beforehand, which is the hard part. Asymmetric encryption uses a pair — the public key encrypts, only the private key decrypts — so no secret need be shared, at the cost of speed. In practice they are combined: asymmetric encryption agrees a key safely, symmetric encryption then carries the bulk of the data.

Integrity and signatures. Hashing, not encryption, guarantees that a message arrived exactly as sent — the distinction matters, since encryption hides a message while integrity proves it was not altered. A digital signature goes further: the sender signs with their private key and anyone can verify with the public key, giving authentication, non-repudiation and integrity together.

long.q: Describe cyber crime and malware, and explain how individuals and organisations can protect themselves.
long.a:
Cyber crime is criminal activity involving a computer, network or the internet — either against computers or using them as the means. Its forms include hacking, identity theft, phishing, credit card fraud, cyber stalking and bullying, intellectual property theft, denial of service, and distributing illegal material. Its effects are financial loss, personal harm that can take years to undo, loss of trust, and — because the internet crosses borders — great difficulty in prosecution. That jurisdictional gap is a large part of why it persists.

Malware is software that harms a system. A virus attaches to a host file and needs a human action to run; it spreads through shared or downloaded files. A worm spreads across the network by itself, needing neither a host file nor a human action. A Trojan is disguised as something legitimate and does not replicate. Spyware watches and reports rather than destroying. Ransomware encrypts files and demands payment for the key. Spam is not malware, but it is a common way of delivering it, and much of it is phishing.

Protection for organisations. Clear policies and procedures; an incident-response plan; documentation of the measures already in place; two-factor authentication, activated on every account that offers it; verbal verification of requests to send money; and an intrusion detection system.

Protection for individuals. Keep the operating system and applications updated — most attacks exploit known faults for which a fix already exists. Run current antivirus software. Use strong, unique passwords, which a password manager makes practical, and enable two-factor authentication. Treat unexpected links and attachments with suspicion, even from people you know. Back up regularly and keep one backup disconnected, so ransomware cannot reach it. Use a firewall, be cautious on public wireless networks, and install software only from sources you trust.

Conclusion. Complete security is not achievable, and claims otherwise should be treated with suspicion. The realistic aim is defence in depth: several measures, so that the failure of one does not expose everything.
